title: The Ravens Won't Win Anything Until They Get Legit Outside Receivers
full_text:
The Ravens have been a failure at evaluating pass rushers and defensive backs under general manager Eric DeCosta, but don’t forget about wide receiver, as well.
Two-time MVP Lamar Jackson can do more with less, and he has throughout his entire career, but with no more guaranteed years on his contract and with the superstar holding complete and total leverage over this organization in 2027 and about to make over $70M/season no matter where he goes, now would be a good time for The Castle to get real about its deep receiver rot.
Zay Flowers is a great piece and he can do a lot of fun and exciting things. But he can't carry a modern passing game. And with tight end Mark Andrews beyond done, and Baltimore's rookie pass catchers doing nothing to this point (how about making Elijah Sarrat active Monday?), they could face a crisis in 2027.
But his lack of size is and always be a significant issue and he will never show up in the redzone and endzone like the very top receivers do, and trying to funnel a passing game to him on crossers and intermediate stuff is always going to come up empty when it really matters. Even with a football genius like Jackson at quarterback. Eventually, one would think the Ravens might recognize this, then again, stubborn and ego is their very scouting brand.
To this point DeCosta would rather keep playing his former draft busts like Rashod Bateman to pretend to be winning outside receivers and keep loading up on guys who really will only do damage in the slot (like all the pass catchers he drafted in 2026) than change his ways. Maybe he’s incapable of it. Whatever. But these kinds of rosters won’t be good enough - especially with running back Derrick Henry’s days as a 5.5 yards/carry guy long gone – and someone there better embrace that reality quickly.
Hall of Fame quarterback Kurt Warner studies NFL offenses constantly as a game analyst and studio analyst on NFL telecasts, and is perpetually baffled by what the Ravens think they can get away with running Bateman and Devontez Walker out there on the outside and hoping Jackson can get by with those kinds of guys.
Warner seemed pretty frustrated for Jackson (dealing with yet another injury suffered in the pocket ) when I brough up the reality of Baltimore trying this “Zay And Pray” approach to the passing game on “The Daily Flock Show”, with one smaller receiver who warrants real attention and the boundary a wasteland.
“I think we all know what Zay Flowers is and he's really good at what he does,” Warner said, “in the slot, run after catch, you know, the quick throws, all of that stuff. And not that he can't break, big plays, because obviously he makes big plays all the time, but you need those complimentary pieces in your offense, even if they're not great, that, hey, when they want to stack inside, we can go outside and we can win the one-on-one battles.
“When they want to take Zay away in the middle of the field, we've got a guy that can stretch the field and give us some chunk plays to make life easier for us offensively. And, you know, that has been a question for a long time. They've really been built inside out. And they've never really found that outside piece that can be a difference-maker.”
Longtime Ravens defensive coordinator Wink Martindale brought up the same concept when we chatted about this roster “They don’t have any Werewolves,” he exclaimed when comparing Lamar’s weapons to other teams, and especially Joe Burrow with the Bengals. Flowers is a great piece, but as the main thing in a playoff winning offense that’s a big ask.
With Jackson holding all the leverage in negotiations, the Ravens need to recruit him to stay. And what they have to offer right now ain't much.
The state of this offensive roster is doing them no favors and they better have a pretty cogent plan to add a true outside receiver, because there isn’t one on this roster and Lane proving to be that guy is another reach and all DeCosta does is reach for receivers; finding the real thing (modern size/speed demon) has been impossible for him.
“There is something to having what I call an X receiver,” Warner said, “a big body, one-on-one receiver on the backside where we can put our three receivers to the right side and we can have this great concept. But if they go one-on-one on the backside, I know I can go there and win and make the game easier.
“I don't have to read through seven guys over here and get to the right read and make the throw. I can go back here and go, ‘Boom, take it!’ You know, throw it to him … Can be a jump ball, but I mean, even just winning on routes, you know, that was what Larry Fitzgerald was for me. You That was what, you know, Tory Holt was for me. If they want to push over here to Isaac (Bruce) and, you know, three receiver sets, I know that I have a great chance to win one-on-one on the backside and get a favorable matchup, and it just makes the game easier for all of us.
It's just go back and pitch and catch, you know, with that guy. And teams havie that guy as a difference-maker for their quarterbacks and especially if you don't have Lamar Jackson and you have a backup quarterback, man, it would be nice to be able to give them some easy completions here and there. And that's been something that, you know, they haven't seemed to have for as long as I can remember is a guy that can do that.”
Under DeCosta, perhaps they never will.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: Top 4 Reasons The Chargers Could Upset The Ravens Monday Night
full_text:
Monday night is a must-win game for the Baltimore Ravens if they want any chance to pretend to be a playoff team.
A win over the winless Chargers isn’t going to provide some huge boost, mind you, and reaching the postseason will remain a stretch given the realities of this roster (it’s just not very good) and this coaching staff (overmatched thus far, by and large ). But a loss would be nothing short of damning, it would beg real questions about the present and future of this failing franchise and could perhaps further grease the path for two-time MVP quarterback Lamar Jackson to decide to ply his trade elsewhere in 2027.
The Chargers have absolutely been the worst team in the NFL, they have earned that 0-8 record and they seem to have absolutely nothing going for them in any aspect of play, and particularly on offense. Traveling across the country on Monday night is probably not their preference right about now. But don’t think for one minute they can’t win this football game, and, believe it or not, they have several things working in their favor above and beyond the fact that Jacoby Brissett will become the fourth quarterback to start a game for the Ravens this season when he takes over in the huddle in Week 9.
Here are the top reasons why the Chargers could pull this off:
Minter looks horribly out of his depth so far, even messaging information about Jackson’s injuries has been a struggle and having his notes out on Monday to hint at lineup changes isn’t much of a bad cop routine. His veteran roster has walked all over him and his young assistants and he’s facing his mentor, in Jim Harbaugh, who knows his psyche and basically created him. The Chargers have nothing to lose and years of practicing against Minter’s defense in college and the NFL means Harbaugh knows a lot of buttons to push.
No one on Minter's staff exudes any real confidence – defensive coordinator Anthony Weaver has become exceptional at suggesting false confidence – they lack leaders and playmakers on both sides of the ball and expecting them to emerge now under extreme duress in a “can’t-lose game,” strikes me as problematic. Minter has been unable to inspire them to this point and they are incredibly weak, mentally, coming off four straight losses.
Minter was asked about trying to coach and call plays at the same time this week, as he should have been. But he seems shaken, and I don't fancy him against his mentor ( major coaching changes should be on the table now, as longtime Raiders exec Amy Trask suggested to us on "The Daily Flock").
This team is 3-9 in its last 12 at home and their choke gene is even more active at home than on the road. They are incredibly adept at getting DeCosta-ed – (blowing a 10-point lead in the second half to lose) at home, and no lead is safe … Oh and they also aren’t built to play from behind having to turn to yet another QB with a 30-year-old offensive coordinator, Declan Doyle, who has struggled to concoct anything that woks in the second half of games.
The front office is acting in a desperate and panicky mode and general manager Eric DeCosta really only builds choking rosters without many players who show up in the clutch. All of this bleeds into the locker room and the bloated payroll and it's an ugly concoction. And then instead of actual introspection, they throw around hollow words like "culture" and mythologize their past. Yuck.
It's like they are built to self-destruct by executives who really only know how to self -destruct from an Ozzie Newsome personnel family tree that has yet to product a single success as a GM.
Baltimore has lost four straight home prime time games, and the Ravens are going to be expected to discard with the worst team in football. Says here that won’t exactly bring out the best in them by a long shot. Collectively, they have a knack for coming up small, and all the weight is on them. Chargers season is already over.
Justin Herbert is not the worst QB in the NFL. He isn’t.
But that's how he's played this far.
Hall of Fame QB Kurt Warner laid out why he believes the star is struggling so mightily and much of it is how he is being asked to read the field with “pure progressions.” At some point Herbert is going to start ignoring his charlatan coordinator, Mike McDaniel, and do what he wants, how he wants. And Harbaugh is going to start getting on the headset and overruling things or taking over play calling himself.
Wouldn’t be surprised at all if that starts Monday night, whether it gets out publicly or not. Something has to change, sitting in Week 10 with 6 touchdown passes and 11 picks is probably rock bottom (QB rating of 75, and after that there is nowhere to go but up. Herbert knows Minter’s tendencies and defaults as well as anyone – certainly better than McDaniel – and I suspect he exhibits more autonomy against his old coach.
The Chargers got a look at Brissett in Week 1,  when the Cardinals pulled off an upset that no longer looks like an upset. Moving to a new team midseason is brutal – and doing it with a team fighting for its season at 4-5, is even tougher. The Chargers don’t miss Minter as much as they miss having a remotely competent offense that can run or pass the football.
Defensively, the Chargers are better than the Ravens.
They are far superior in the redzone (11th) and on third-down (8th) and have allowed a lower opposing passer rating for the season, too. The Chargers are also superior to the Ravens in points allowed per drive. Given just how pathetic both of these offensive lines are, there is the potential for big plays to be made on defense, but the relative lack of mobility from Brissett, in comparison to Herbert, could end up being a considerable factor in this game and we expect Herbert’s legs to be a big part of the game plan.
Sad as it is to say, given Minter’s pedigree and how highly the Ravens touted him, the Chargers have the edge on defense and a considerable edge at kicker and that might be enough to win a tight game. They are certainly overdue.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: Ravens Coach Jesse Minter Continues Bizarre Handling Of Lamar Jackson's Status
full_text:
Almost everything about the job of being the Ravens head coach, and replacing John Harbaugh, who was a mainstay with the organization, has been awkward for Jesse Minter.
And even among that backdrop, the rookie coach (and seriously struggling defensive coordinator ) has seemed most uncomfortable messaging about two significant injuries for two-time MVP quarterback Lamar Jackson. Minter chose to call a high-ankle sprain that kept Jackson out for nearly a month a “day-to-day” situation for nearly three weeks, and he was very guarded in revealing anything about Jackson’s thumb injury early this week. Then the team put out an oddly worded statement in Minter’s name Friday addressing Jackson’s injury to some degree and calling in a 6-to-10-week recovery.
Everything about Jackson is always a massive national story, especially his injuries and especially when NFL “insiders” have made a cottage industry out of suggesting Jackson will be back on wildly inaccurate and overly ambitious timelines for years . Minter’s handling of Jackson’s earlier issues already struck many as puzzling and on Saturday he continued the strange rhetorical games when he declined to speak as to when Jackson’s thumb surgery was conducted – which would provide critical context for team’s timeline for his recovery.
It’s one thing to expect the least for a team with four straight losses that has been as bad as any in the history of the franchise - the first to fail to score 14 points in four straight games and the second to allow 33 points or more in three straight ( begging major questions of this staff) . But the exchanges about Jackson’s injury are getting a little surreal for not even 10 games into Minter’s tenure here..
To put out a statement in a coach’s name that goes to lengths not to reveal when the procedure in question took place was always going to require further questioning from the media. When it came on Saturday, here’s what Minter had to say about why they released the statement:
“Really just to kind of get it out there of what happened, again less speculation of timelines and what happened and things like that,” Minter suggested. “Lamar [and I are very much on the same page with the whole thing. Leave it at that."
Of course, Minter was then asked directly when the surgery took place:
"The surgery happened, and the timeline is the timeline," he said, which will only heighten a climate where even more speculation takes place.
Jackson was almost certain to never throw a pass again for the Ravens this season from the moment he suffered the major thumb injury on his first snap of Week 8 – his first game back from the high-ankle sprain. That seems even more clear now, with the offense in disarray (good luck to new starter Jacoby Brissett), the offensive line among the worst in football and the Ravens unable to run the football or protect their quarterbacks (three got hurt in rapid succession in that Buffalo game ).
Jackson will decide whether he wants to stay in Baltimore or not his offseason, with no guaranteed money on his 2027 and a bevy of carefully-curated poison pills he negotiated in his favor – an $84M cap hit, a no-trade clause and a no-tag clause among them. It’s led many to believe he will request another trade early this offseason – including the negotiating expert who helped him broker his last contract -  and he will command over $70M a year on whatever structure he prefers no matter where he plays.
In the meantime, the rampant guessing about everything regarding Jackson will only increase in what is shaping up to be surely yet another lost season for the Ravens .
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: Ravens Must Be Willing To Shake-Up Their Coaching Staff ASAP, Longtime Raiders Team Pres Amy Trask Contends
full_text:
The Jesse Minter hire wasn’t supposed to be some three-year plan.
The Ravens claimed the rookie head coach – clearly under the thumb of the front office regime that wanted a first-time staff – was uniquely positioned to be wise beyond his years because he came from their “winning culture.” He knew their systems and players and was a product of them and their front office and overarching philosophies in many ways. And now, entering the 10th game of this regime, all involved seem woefully out of their depth .
They are fielding a non-competitive football product , and once again raised eyebrows around the NFL at the trade deadline by seemingly pretending they are this contending team that they are not . They want to send a signal that things are largely okay – save for maybe benching a player or two and tweaking the lineup. But to experienced eyes around the football world – former Ravens assistants like Wink Martindale, who created the defensive system Minter is using , and Marvin Lewis, who ran the defense on Baltimore’s first Super Bowl team - big problems are obvious.
And when longtime Raiders team president Amy Trask, now an NFL analyst for CBS Sports, joined me on “The Daily Flock” this week, she made it clear that very much in the Ravens’ front office and coaching staff must be under serious review ASAP. Trask, who saw plenty of upheaval and coaching mistakes during her time with Oakland/Los Angeles, sees some major red flags and in her own understated way, agreed with how overmatched this staff has appeared to be at times, and raised the specter of the need for potential coordinator changes by 2027.
Nothing much seems pointed in the right direction on offense, defense or special teams; 30-year-old offensive coordinator Declan Doyle is as under scrutiny as Minter and general manager Eric DeCosta right now. And with four straight losses, a prediction for blowing leads and most players underachieving, Monday night is a must-win against the winless Chargers and this franchise must start embracing its new realities.
Trask, who was trained by owner Al Davis who knew the game from all angles (including coaching), sees ample cause for concern through this half season.
The fact the Ravens have already blown three games this season in which they held a lead of 10-points or more in the second half (continuing a nasty trend from John Harbaugh’s regime), and that they are the worst second-half team in the NFL (scoring the second-fewest points and allowing the most) must be addressed in a meaningful manner, she contends.
“Take a look at everything,” Trask explained. “Why is that happening? Are they not making good halftime adjustments? Is it a talent? Are there holes on the roster? … Are they doing things in the first half that are tells as is said? …
“Is the opposing team seeing things that they are doing? That is a tell. Is it a training issue? Is it a conditioning issue? Are players wearing out again? Holes in the roster, weaknesses in the roster, or is it coaching? All of that needs to be evaluated.”
As to whether the decision to pair a coaching staff this naïve with a roster this experienced with this heavy of expectations begs corrections, Trask believes corrections are in order.
“I'm a big, big, big, believer when you have a first-time head coach, you need some people around that head coach,” Trask said. “Whether it's an offensive coordinator, a defensive coordinator, an assistant head coach, an adviser to the head coach, you need a seasoned voice in the ear.
“Simply someone who's been through this and may have some observations that a first-time head coach isn't. Look, my college, my Cal bears - first time head coach, first time offensive coordinator, first time defensive coordinator. So, this is something I've been thinking a lot, as relates to my Golden Bears, who I will always love no matter the record …
“And I'll tell you, I would not be surprised if this is something the Ravens do. I wouldn't be the least bit surprised - and I would expect that they would do this - if not before then, then in the off season. Even if they retain the offensive and defensive coordinators, bring in someone senior as a defensive adviser and offensive adviser, both.  But bring some seniority in there that can give some um seasoned perspective.”
We called for reaching out to Lewis or Martindale weeks ago. We’d be shocked if the Ravens reacted in season now and made any move this bold. We agree with Trask, whole-heartedly, that considering different voices calling plays next season must be in order if this team is going to try to reach the postseason in what could be Lamar Jackson's last season in Baltimore , at all costs.
They also are going to be hard pressed not to make significant alterations to the composition of this staff barring quick and sweeping improvement, no matter what.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: Jacoby Brissett Compares Learning Ravens Offense To Crash Course Ahead Of Debut
full_text:
Since landing in Maryland late last week after being acquired by the Baltimore Ravens in a trade with the Arizona Cardinals in exchange for a 2027 fourth-round pick and a 2028 seventh-round pick, veteran quarterback Jacoby Brissett has been dialed in on learning the playbook and building chemistry with his new teammates.
Head coach Jesse Minter declared him the team's starter for their Week 10 primetime matchup against the Los Angeles Chargers earlier this week after he spent last weekend around the building with offensive coordinator Declan Doyle and other support staff getting up to speed.
"It's definitely a crash course," Brissett said.." No question. [I want to] really just come out, try to do my job to the best of my ability, be a good teammate, kind of keep things simple [and] try not to overcomplicate this thing right now and just take it one day at a time."
Brissett feels confident about the progress he's made in learning the offense and building chemistry with his new teammates, but knows there's plenty more prep work to do to ensure they are successful and can consistently execute the game plan at a high level.
"I don't think my preparation is stopping today, but I think I have the right coaches that are helping me along the way. Obviously, the players are helping me when I'm in the huddle and things of that nature, so it's been good. Like I said, I feel confident, but obviously [there's] still some work to do."
Following each of the Ravens' first two practices of the week, he spent an extended period on the field throwing to some of the team's top targets in the passing game, including two-time Pro Bowl wide receiver Zay Flowers, talented rookie wideout Ja'Kobi Lane and vertical speedster Devontez Walker.
"It's just going through the plan," Brissett said. "We do a bunch of walk-throughs. You see the practice, stuff after practice and things of that nature. I just think it's that, and then just them telling me what they need from me more than I need from them. They have to do the hard part. I have to do the easy part and find them and put the ball where it's supposed to go. It's just [about] the communication on both sides."
His arrival and insertion into the starting lineup will undoubtedly be a major boost for Flowers, who has only logged three catches for six receiving yards on 11 targets in the past two games after averaging just over 101 receiving yards in his first six appearances. Given Brissett's prowess as an accurate passer over the middle of the field and at the intermediate level, Lane could finally get a chance to live up to the training camp and preseason buzz he built up.
"He's a guy who's played 11 years, so he's seen a lot of football," Doyle said. "He's seen a lot of these pictures, and he'll let it rip. He can really drive the ball. Those are all things that I'm really excited about with him."
Brissett's first impressions of Doyle have been similar to those of so many others who've crossed paths with him during his ascension up the coaching ranks and since he landed his first play-calling role in Baltimore.
"He's a great football mind," Brissett said. "He's been very receptive to information from me and getting to know each other, whether that's on the field and off the field and trying to bridge the gap over a relationship that you kind of have to fast-track before Monday.
"But he's been awesome. What he's thinking as far as the play structure and then obviously how we're attacking the defense, he's very vocal about it. I think that cleans up the communication. I know what he's thinking."
Even before the Ravens and Minter issued an official statement on Friday, confirming the reports on the exact nature of franchise quarterback Lamar Jackson's thumb injury and outlining a timeline for a potential return this season , Brissett wasn't concerned with how long he'd have the reins of the offense.
"I don't even really want to get into it," Brissett said. "It's one of those things where you kind of just take it day by day, and then future things happen when future things happen. But, I'd be a fool to look forward. I'm trying to learn teammates, players, coaches, plays and get ready for a game. The last thing I'm worried about is something that's going to happen down the road."
The Ravens mark the seventh different team that the journeyman backup and stop-gap starter will have played for in his 11-year career, and this isn't the first time he's been traded for by a team looking to salvage their season. He was acquired by the Indianapolis Colts ahead of the 2017 season after their then-franchise quarterback Andrew Luck suffered a shoulder injury that caused him to miss the entire year.
Over the course of his career, he's compiled a record as a starter of 23-50 and has played in several different offensive systems, which he believes has made him very adaptable to being thrust into new environments.
"I think that's just it. You are around a lot of different people, a lot of different systems, different situations, every year," Brissett said. "Just being able to be flexible, that's what's kept me in this league for so long, and this is no different. [I'm] just excited for this opportunity, and [I'm] trying to make the most of it."

title: The Ravens Will Regret Not Trading Derrick Henry To The Giants, Among Others
full_text:
Former Ravens head coach John Harbaugh was on the prowl for an impact running back at the trade deadline. He never hid it.
He went on the record about calling Titans ownership himself about trying to land some of their top players and the Giants made it pretty clear they had a second-round pick and at least a fifth-round pick on the table for Colts star running back Jonathan Taylor. And when they pulled out of those talks because the price was so high, numerous league sources indicated the Giants had very real interest in Ravens running back Derrick Henry as well.
Because of course they did . Harbaugh had the young Giants ahead of where most expected, while Ravens rookie coach Jesse Minter's team is clearly not a contender as the rest of the league sees it.
Harbaugh saw Henry at his best for two years in Baltimore and he and his run-game guy, Greg Roman (remember him?) know what a guy like Henry can do in option looks with a young, nimble running quarterback (like New York starter JJ McCarthy). Henry’s salary was no issue at all (the Giants were pursuing numerous stars making way more money)
“It’s got to be something that is a need, that fits your financial profile, that fits your price tag,” Harbaugh said of New York’s trade pursuits ahead of the deadline. Henry (prorated $1.3M case salary) did, but the Ravens sent strong signals to the marketplace all along that they would not move the slumping 32-year-old. The national media drove that narrative home and Baltimore did nothing but make panic moves at the deadline (fleeced by the Eagles for struggling lineman Cam Jurgens) and gave a kicker away, somehow, at the same time.
For a team without it’s second-round pick in 2028 (Jurgens) and dealing fourth-round value for quarterback Jacoby Brissett and short on 2027 picks already, this tactic will prove regrettable, like most of the decisions made in The Castle the last three years. Here’s why:
Multiple general managers told us Henry carried fourth-down value and if the Ravens had marketed him as they should, and played a few teams off each other, that was the floor. Getting more was never out of the question. I asked multiple personnel execs about what they thought they could get for him in the offseason - without the heat of the playoff push spurring suitors, with Henry then 33, and especially if he continues the rapid downward spiral of this season (more on that in a minute).
“If they didn’t trade him now, they aren’t trading him,” one GM suggested. “They aren’t getting anything (of value) next year. That ship sailed.”
One personnel exec with a team that was active ahead of the deadline said: “This was the time to trade him. Not in March. He won't have a market in March”
And our pal Mark Levin, who ran the salary cap and agent administration department for the NFLPA for roughly 25 years and who knows contracts and cap as well as anyone, after studying the Ravens ugly payroll/cap situation, came to the same conclusion. Levin, who oversaw the cap and contract negotiations for the Washington Commanders before going to the NFLPA, would have been pushing his front office to trade Henry at the deadline
“His value will probably not be any higher than it is right now,” Levin pointed out on “The Daily Flock,” while explaining why he believes Lamar Jackson will be elsewhere in 2027 . And, after not moving Henry, it seems clear to Levin after studying all the contract ramifications that: “I would lean probably towards keeping him (in 2027), if you don't trade him like right now.”
And ESPN reports the Ravens essentially told Henry as much ahead of the deadline.
So what does that mean moving forward?
Well, if Jackson isn’t here the run game is cooked no matter what. The offensive line has massive issues interior and at left tackle moving forward, the move to an under-center rushing attack has been totally thwarted. The Ravens are just 13th in under-center rushes and without Jackson those carries average a pedestrian 4.1 yards/carry.
Henry is being mauled at or behind the line of scrimmage like never before – again, the line is terrible all the way around – unable to get up a head of steam to be explosive. He is averaging just 3.4 yards per carry over the last month, he has been run as much as back in the NFL despite his advanced age, this is nothing like the 5.5/rush he averaged his first two years here and at this stage of his career Henry needs others to lift him up so.
Impossible with this roster.
Rookie offensive coordinator Declan Doyle has run Henry 175 times through nine games – third-most through Week 9 for a 32-year-old RB since the 1970 AFL/NFL merger . Only Walter Payton and Otis Anderson have carried it more at that age, and that was ancient history in terms of NFL offensive philosophy. In the last six weeks Henry has run 109 times for just 388 yards (3.6 yards/carry) with just two touchdown runs and a putrid 0.67 yards before contract.
“They can keep running him into a brick wall, but he’s not going to run through it,” said an NFL exec who has advanced the Ravens this season, noting the need for them to incorporate more speed backs and different looks out of the pistol, with no ability to run inside or under center with Henry.
And as longtime NFL general manager Marty Hurney, who watches the Ravens closely for "The Daily Flock," pointed out to us on numerous occasions, "the fumbling has me a little concerned, too."
Perhaps, these are all adjustments they’ll get around to making a year too late in 2027. But Doyle seems intent on getting his 300 carries out of Henry this season, and whatever he looks like for the remainder of his career in Baltimore, the hubris of the 2026 trade deadline is quite likely to always carry a price for a rebuilding team come February
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: Ravens Finally Provide Update And Timeline On Lamar Jackson's Return
full_text:
After refusing to address anything regarding two-time MVP quarterback Lamar Jackson’s latest significant injury this week, the Baltimore Ravens finally provided an update Friday morning.
Rookie head coach Jesse Minter, who was criticized for calling Jackson’s high-ankle sprain a “day-to-day” situation for nearly three weeks, would not answer questions this week about Jackson’s thumb injury suffered in Week 8. Minter would not comment on the specifics of the injury or whether any procedure had taken place. On Friday, with the Ravens having an unusual media schedule than normal this week with a Monday night game following a Thursday game, the team finally added context to the situation.
The Ravens released a statement from Minter (still nothing from the team president or general manager) saying the following:
“Lamar is doing well as he recovers from the broken and dislocated thumb injury he suffered in Week 8.
“Recovery timelines are challenging to predict, but injuries like this that require surgery typically take about 6-10 weeks to heal. He is doing everything he can to get back, and we will let his progress guide the timing of his return.
“We are committed to playing our best football over the second half of the season.”
The wording of the statement is much more coy than it needs to be. It does not specify if surgery was absolutely conducted, but hints at it. And it suggests a wide timeline based off returning from a procedure but doesn't note exactly when it was conducted (or, frankly that it was conducted).
Jackson was injured on his first dropback after coming back from the ankle injury, one of three Ravens quarterbacks injured in rapid succession in that game, in the pocket, behind an offensive line in constant decline that is begging real questions about the acumen of this front office . The Ravens generally do not make players available to the media while on Injured Reserve – where Jackson was placed last week.
Jackson’s injuries are always the subject of rampant media speculation, which almost always projects ridiculously ambitious timetables . And so it was again, starting days after this latest injury, and for the team not to address this in some manner would have been ridiculous with the player himself not in position to meet the media. It remains highly unlikely that Jackson plays another game this season, for myriad reasons.
Baltimore’s playoff hopes are slim; the team has lost four straight games while outscored 117-43, it has just two AFC wins thus far (with among the worst strength of victory tiebreakers in the conference) and is 7-15 starting games without Jackson since he became their starter in 2018. The Ravens will not be favored in many games down the stretch and are hoping Jacoby Brissett, just demoted to third string with rebuilding Arizona, can stabilize a failing run game and passing attack (it should help some pass catchers , but not enough).
Jackson coming back in December, having last played a full football game Week 3 – in Brazil – is highly unlikely under normal circumstances. This being the Ravens, the circumstances are anything but normal and the combination of him having no more guarantees in his contract and no future injury protections, with a stable of poison pills in his favor, make this effectively the end of his season.
Jackson has the leverage to decide where he plays next season, and putting him back out there under there circumstances to risk further medical issues would be silly for player and team (this is the worst second-half team in the NFL with a coaching staff that’s yet to remotely show it is ready for all of this). The Ravens best tread lightly with this player, whom some with unique access and insight into his prior negotiations with this franchise already believe is headed elsewhere in 2027.
Having Jackson hurt going into the offseason would only hurt his trade value, and at this point it would be malfeasance – like giving away a starting kicker for no good reason – for the Ravens not to be considering such variables.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: Ravens Provide Clarification On Surprising Last-Second Trade Acquisition
full_text:
It's rare to see a team make a trade for two starters at the same position where only one player can be on the field at a time without there having been a significant injury occur between the time both were acquired.
However, after losing all three of their top centers that they added during he offseason to major injuries before Week 4 rolled around, who can blame the Baltimore Ravens for wanting to upgrade and bolster the depth of their interior offensive line with another center?
Nonetheless, general manager Eric DeCosta's decision to pull the trigger on a trade right at the deadline for former Atlanta Falcons starting center Ryan Neuzil , barely over a month after trading a 2028 second-round pick to the Philadelphia Eagles for two-time Pro  Bowler Cam Jurgens , was a little puzzling for fans and pundits to take in .
Instant reactions to the move ranged from speculating whether Neuzil was coming in to be inserted into the starting lineup sooner rather than later, whether it be at center and slide Jurgens over to left guard, or if he'd straight up replace inconsistent veteran John Simpson at guard. He has started each of the last nine games at center for the Falcons and came into the league as a former All American at guard.
"I think he brings versatility," head coach Jesse Minter said. "I don't anticipate anything changing with Cam [Jurgens] and what position he plays, and we think he's the future of our offensive line. I think it's just a piece that adds depth, and I do think he'll have some position flexibility as he gets here and as he gets going. Wherever that leads, I think we'll see as we go."
Before becoming a Raven, Jurgens was playing out of position at guard for the Eagles and experienced some struggles. He is glad to be back in this natural position on a new team and welcomes Neuzil's arrival and what it means for the overall quality and depth of his unit.
"It's never a bad thing to have more guys that can snap," Jurgens said. "Ryan's a guy that's played a lot of football. I'm excited to have him in the room."
By adding a player of Neuzil's experience, versatility and pedigree, the Ravens won't find themselves in a position of having to slide stud first-round rookie Vega Ioane over to center again and leave them with another subpar combination at guard. It also gives them another option to turn to at left guard if Simpson's play doesn't improve.
To go from starting nearly 30 straight games to being relegated to a high-value backup is not what Neuzil envisioned for himself when the season started, and he was the anchor in the middle of his own unit, but he's willing to play whatever role is required of him.
"I'm not sure really the plan right now," Neuzil said. "I'm just here to get better and fill in wherever they need me to...I played a little bit of guard my first year, and then transitioned to center, but just wherever they need me."
The last few days have been a bit of a whirlwind for the sixth-year veteran and his family as he went from returning home from playing in the Falcons' international matchup with the Cincinnati Bengals in Spain on Sunday to hopping on a plane to Baltimore late Tuesday night.
Unlike most players who are brought in from another team in the middle of the season, Neuzil has a strong foundation in the type of wide-zone blocking schemes that he'll be executing in Baltimore. He spent the first four years of his career being groomed by Ravens offensive line coach and run game coordinator Dwayne Ledford, who was likely consulted by the player personnel department in before the trade was made.
"It definitely helps a lot," Neuzil said. "I was with [Ledford] for five years in Atlanta, so [I] understand what he wants and what he sees in offensive linemen, so it's definitely a plus."

title: Forget The Playoffs: Can The Ravens Achieve These 5 Lesser Goals In Final 8 Games?
full_text:
The Baltimore Ravens are one of the more deficient football teams in the NFL right now.
They have allowed four more touchdowns than they have scored this season and been outscored by nearly 70 points in the last four games alone. They have almost no ascending players and coaches on either roster. Their first half was a failure and playing the rest of the season without two-time MVP Lamar Jackson, almost certainly the case , is a recipe for disaster (7-15 without him).
This was a rebuilding year all along with a coaching staff that appears to be mightily out of its depth thus far and that’s unlikely to change under the pressure of trying to salvage a season with a QB who was just demoted to third string in Arizona, where they are absolutely rebuilding. As much as everyone in The Castle seems utterly delusional about the state of this franchise and how far removed it is for competing or anything real (even with a healthy Jackson), as evidenced by their abysmal trade deadline , we keep it real in these parts.
So, the standings and postseason are not going to be our guide anymore. We are setting hopes and expectations far below that standard (let alone the Super Bowl talk going around Owings Mills as the AFC’s preseason favorite). Nope, we are more concerned with five far lesser objective for the rest of the season.
Let’s see if this flailing organization can manager to check a few of these boxes:
This can’t be the “Zay And Pray” passing game forever. They sunk the middle of this draft into receivers and tight ends – can one of them have a half-meaningful rookie season? That too much to ask? Can Ja’Kobi Lane or Matthew Hibner or Josh Cuevas show enough in some regular-season NFL football games that make you feel good about their ability to make an impact in 2027?
Rookie offensive coordinator Declan Doyle is underwater in many respects, but player development is supposed to be where these young coaches would succeed where John Harbaugh, owner Steve Bisciotti put it, failed (real problem is the GM is pretty awful at his job, but the owner claims he “bats .800” ). Somebody from this group has to show something with Jacoby Brissett slinging it downfield in games that won’t end up meaning much in the standings.
“I can do a better job of putting them in better positions and making sure that they're able to go out and execute,” Doyle said of his players last week. This offense will be cooked next season unless one of these youngsters is legit.
Hamilton is not a playmaker on passing downs in any way shape or form. They don’t need another run stuffer – that’s all they have on this defense. Let’s see him affect he QB before he delivers the ball or after it, being around the football in flight. This was supposed to be the embodiment of Jesse Minter’s next-level defense, and it’s been anything but .
Slamming him into offensive linemen and running backs and hanging out in the blue tent every Sunday feels like a dangerous game to be playing in a lost season. Fashion a role for him that makes more impact, that hopefully can carry into next season.
“If I'm out there, I need to be putting good stuff out there on tape,” Hamilton said after the ugly loss to the Bills in Week 8. “Me, myself personally, I don't think I did that. Doesn't matter the situation I'm in. If I'm out there, I need to be doing my best to get the job done."
Minter talked on Monday about “re-establishing” key tenants on his defense. Sorry, outside of consistently proving to be the worst second-half defense in the NFL and displaying an unrivaled ability to blow any second-half lead at any time, Minter hasn’t established anything here as a coach or coordinator.
He better establish an identity, fast, or get ready to keep fielding more questions about horrendous second-half play calling and lack of adjustments . His secondary stinks and his pass rush is limp and his dime coverages are picked apart by bad QBs and he doesn’t get home when he blitzes … They can stop the run some, but who cares when the middle of the field is always wide open in the passing game.
“A couple days gives you a chance to really look and really dig deep,” Minter said after a weekend off. “I think first and foremost, making sure that the identity that we talk about that we want is not just talk. Sometimes that can get lost as you're racing each week to try to get a game plan in and do things. I'm excited for us to sort of re-establish our identity.”
Good luck with that with this roster.
Could anyone besides linebacker Trenton Simpson make the case for a new contract? Too much to ask? Can’t have a team with only three blue-chip players signed beyond 2027 (Nnamdi Madubuike, Hamilton, Flowers) and no one else you need to pay at the same time. Won’t work.
That would be a sign of a bogus front office.
Simpson should be groomed to replace Roquan Smith, now, and every effort made to pay him, now . Will anyone else – Nate Wiggins, Devontez Walker – be performing at a level that would make you want to do the same by January? I wouldn’t bet on it.
The Ravens have championed their roster for years, and the media carries their water, but it’s not very good with massive room for improvement. Now under .500 by some margin since last Thanksgiving, they get better active on waiver claims.
How about finding a player that way? How about plundering someone who can play a little on another practice squad? How about constantly churning the bottom of the roster the way bad football teams do – this has been a bad football team for quite a while. Living off a false reputation and constantly firing coaches who are scapegoated for poor rosters is one thing; doing almost nothing to help them in-season (outside of ridiculously desperate trades that will only set the entire franchise back just makes it even worse.
“When’s the last time they found a football player on a Tuesday?” offered one longtime NFL personnel exec, noting the workouts to fill roster spots that usually take place that day. “Do they think that’s beneath them too? Like (selling at) the trade deadline?
“There’s never anybody on waivers who is better than their 53? When’s the last time they stole somebody who could play off a practice squad? What do the pro personnel guys do over there?”
They might be fooling the access jockeys in the media, and the people who grade offseasons and drafts. But not their peers around the league and any veteran evaluators really paying attention, who see right through this failing front office.
Jason has covered sports professionally for newspapers, websites and broadcast networks since 1996 and have covered the NFL extensively for The Washington Post, CBS Sports and The NFL Network from 2004-2025.

title: Are Roquan Smith, Derrick Henry, Mark Andrews Back With Ravens in '27? NFL Contract Expert Predicts
full_text:
The Ravens’ ugly payroll and salary-cap situation is born primarily of their inability to act like a functional NFL front office when it comes to extending the contract of their franchise quarterback.
Lamar Jackson has been forced to take a truly unique negotiating path through roughly a decade in the NFL, and it’s not because he chose to represent himself (something increasingly common place in his locker room and around the NFL). Baltimore is staring at a $75M dead cap on Jackson for 2027, and an $84M cap hit is he plays out the final year on his deal with all those poison pills, with no easy way out.
Our pal Mark Levin, who ran the salary cap and agent administration department for the NFLPA for roughly 25 years (as foremost an expert on NFL contracts and structure and cap and the collective bargain agreement as there is on the planet), was also quite involved in Jackson’s last contract with the Ravens. And he explained why there is every reason to be skeptical about Jackson’s future in Baltimore after this season.
But Levin, who ran the salary cap and was the chief negotiator for the Washington Commanders prior to taking the role with the NFLPA, also spent hours recently pouring over Baltimore’s entire current and future cap situation and studying the critical contracts while trying to find ways to get Baltimore under the 2027 cap (they project $50M over it currently ).
Levin, who took a buyout from the union and now runs Pro Football Consulting assisting agents negotiating deals, knows how general managers and cap gurus and owners think and he has a unique portal into Baltimore’s front office from being on the inside of Jackson’s last deal. He also explained on “The Daily Flock” what he thinks the Ravens will do with a score of other pressing contract matters (Roquan Smith, Ronnie Stanley, Derrick Henry, Mark Andrews, Rashod Bateman).
PSA: Marlon Humphrey isn’t in this exercise because he is a UFA in 2027, but he’ll still count $12M against Baltimore’s cap either way; quite a parting gift).
·       Pre 6/1 (Cut/ Trade): $13M ( Save $20M )  / $13M ( Save $20M )
·       Post 6/1 (Cut/Trade): $13M ( Save $20M) / $32M ( Save $20M )
·       Base Salary: $15M  ($4M bonus due March)
Smith has been in steep decline for years, and Trenton Simpson is the rare player making the case for a contract extension on this roster, who might be the next-man up. Smith is being paid like Fred Warner and he is worth maybe a third of that and has a cap hit $14M higher than anyone else in the NFL at his position. He’ll be 30 with 3000 snaps under his belt come ’27 and mobility and acceleration have become a big issue.
Levin: “They're not gonna pay a player four million and then cut him. They're gonna cut him before they have to pay the four million.”
Prediction : They offer Smith a bargain 2027 contract and he declines becoming a free agent at start of league year.
Suggestion: Now’s the time see what Simpson, Teddye Buchanan and Kyle Hamilton can do on the field together (30 snaps all season thus far).
·       2027 Cap/Dead Cap: $24M / $28M
·       Pre 6/1 (Cut/ Trade): $28M / $28M
·       Post 6/1 (Cut/Trade): $8M ( Save $16M ) / $8M ( Save $16M )
He thought his career might be over years ago and extreme medical concerns led him to come back to Baltimore with no real market in free agency. His play is declining, left tackle is a massive need in the draft and the voidable years have made this a brutal cap bind. But remember, cash is king, owner Steve Biscciotti is paying a team-record $370M for his awful product this year, and shedding that $16M base salary is a big deal.
Levin : “Ronnie Stanley would be somebody that you might be able to absorb that extra $4 million hit (from $24M to $28M) and just cut him right away in March.”
Prediction: I could see them saving the $4M and designating him a post-June 1 cut and letting him test the market early.
Suggestion : Don’t get cute in the draft and wait to draft a successor with this awful OL a constant problem.
·       2027 Cap/Dead Cap: $16M / $15M
·       Pre 6/1 (Cut/ Trade): $15M / $15M
·       Post 6/1 (Cut/Trade): $12M ( Save $4M ) / $12M ( Save $4M)
·       Base Salary: $11M ($1M Bonus Due March)
He will be 33, beyond the end for almost everyone who has ever played his position and he’s being ridden into the ground by rookie offensive coordinator Declan Doyle this year. Without a quality OL and Lamar Jackson, he doesn’t really fit, but the fact this front office wouldn’t do the obvious thing and deal him at the deadline was telling, too. The fumbles are a growing concern.
Levin: “I would lean probably towards keeping him.
Prediction: The King is back in 2027, even on a rebuilding team.
Suggestion: Find a viable complimentary back worthy of 10-15 touches a game
·       2027 Cap/Dead Cap: $15M / $16M
·       Pre 6/1 (Cut/ Trade): $16M / $11M (Save $4M )
·       Post 6/1 (Cut/Trade): $16M / $11M ( Save $4M )
·       Base Salary: $9M ($5M fully guaranteed)
The decision to take the money Isaiah Likely turned down in negotiations last season – wanting to see what the market would bear (perfectly logical and reasonable by Likely) – is the kind of thing that gets you fired by an engaged owner who is driven to win (this one gaslights fans about a GM he says “bats .800” on his transactions). It was a petty and bratty move in realtime and has come to exemplify how this team operates. Andrews is one of the worst tight ends in the NFL the last two season and he cannot run, jump or catch, but leads the NFL in drop percentage at his position and false starts.
Levin: “They could possibly trade him, but I would think more likely he's probably going to be on their roster next year.”
Prediction: They couldn’t get a 4th round pick for him after 2024, when he was just a marginal TE but not a broken one. No trade, and the $5M guarantee means he’s back. He also will retire without a playoff TD in his career.

title: DJ Moore Finally Shakes Injury Status, Appears Ready for Takeoff for Bills in Week 10
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills listed five offensive starters on their official Week 10 injury report , but for the first time in seven weeks, there was one particular name missing.
Bills' top wide receiver DJ Moore appears to have finally returned to full strength, nearly two full months after suffering a shoulder injury against the Detroit Lions on September 17.
Moore had been appearing daily on the injury report since the Week 3 game against the Los Angeles Chargers.
Even last week, prior to the Monday Night Football road win, the Bills slow played the situation by limiting Moore's practice participation and keeping him in a red non-contact jersey. He did not, however, carry a designation heading into kickoff, and the wide receiver recorded 47 snaps (59 percent share).
Then, as the Bills opened the practice week on Wednesday, Moore was a full go on Wednesday as preparations for the New York Jets kicked off.
Moore's shoulder separation was not supposed to be a long-term issue. In fact, he was available in Week 3 against the Chargers, only 10 days removed from suffering the injury.
It was during the Week 4 game against the New England Patriots when Moore was knocked off track. He reaggravated the injury while falling to the ground trying to make a catch near the sideline.
Much to Moore's chagrin, the Bills held their WR1 out in Weeks 5 and 6 heading into a Week 7 bye.
"The two weeks [out], it was pretty sad. I was mad at myself," said Moore coming off the bye. "I don't be wanting to miss time. I be wanting to be out there with the guys."
After missing game action for the first time since December 2020, Moore returned for the Week 8 home game against the Baltimore Ravens on November 1.
He made four receptions for 82 yards and one touchdown against Baltimore, and he also avoided a potential knee problem in his final catch.
When the Bills visit the Jets for a 1 p.m. ET kickoff on November 15, the offense will appear that much more dangerous with a true deep threat who opens up opportunities for others.
"He gives us that downfield presence, the run after the catch stuff," said quarterback Josh Allen.
As advertised, Moore made a 49-yard reception on a 50-50 ball against the Ravens. In Week 9, Buffalo used him one a couple wide receiver screens, one of which was scored as an 11-yard rush.
"Obviously, we know the importance that he brings to our football team, to our offense, the toughness, the playmaking ability. It'll be nice to get him back out on the football field today," said head coach Joe Brady during Ravens week.
For the injury-interrupted season, Moore has 19 receptions for 285 yards and two touchdowns. He has rushed four times for 20 yards, too.

title: Bills' Last Game vs. Jets' Geno Smith Combo Brings Back Motown Memories
full_text:
Buffalo Bills fans of the early-to-mid-2010s may remember Geno Smith's first go-around with the New York Jets, and on Sunday, Buffalo will get another shot at Gang Green with Smith as its quarterback .
The last time Smith took significant snaps against Buffalo as a member of the Jets, the Bills weren't at Ralph Wilson Stadium, as the Bills' old stadium was known at the time, or MetLife Stadium.
Present-day Bills fans may remember them winning twice at Ford Field in Detroit in five days in 2022, but that wasn't the first time Buffalo won twice in the Motor City in the same season.
In 2014, the November 13-21 blizzard moved the Bills' Week 12 game against the Jets from Buffalo to Detroit. Buffalo, which had beaten the Lions earlier in the year, entered at 5-5, while New York was 2-8.
What followed was a complete drubbing in one of the most satisfying games of the 2014 season, a year in which the Bills fell just short of breaking the longest postseason drought by an NFL team at the time.
What carried the Bills was their defense, a unit that led the NFL with 54 sacks that season. Michael Vick started at quarterback for New York, and Buffalo sacked him seven times. Jerry Hughes and Mario Williams each had two sacks, while Kyle Williams, Ty Powell and Nickell Robey-Coleman chipped in with one each.
The defense forced Vick into an interception and several other near-picks, which sent him to the bench for Smith, who was 10-of-12 for 89 yards, albeit when the game was out of reach thanks to some nice complementary football akin to what the 2026 Bills have played lately .
Buffalo's offense, which was led by quarterback Kyle Orton during his swan song, put up consistent points with the help of a big special teams play to pull away in this one.
Orton went 24-of-32 for 230 yards and two touchdowns, one to Robert Woods and the other to Scott Chandler. Woods had nine receptions on the day, three times as much as the next-closest receiver, which he turned into 118 yards and his touchdown.
On the ground, Fred Jackson and Anthony "Boobie" Dixon each found the end zone, but the biggest play of the game came on special teams, with Manny Lawson blocking a punt and recovering it in the end zone for a touchdown that all but put the game away at 24-3.
The final score wound up 38-3, a score very similar to the Bills' last game at the old Highmark Stadium .
If the Bills can rattle Smith like they did Vick on that day in Detroit, they should be able to cruise to victory rather easily and improve to 8-1, keeping pace for the AFC's top seed.

title: Five Key Things to Know About Bills vs. Jets in Week 10
full_text:
It’s been roughly six weeks since the first-place Buffalo Bills suffered their only loss of the season.
Joe Brady’s unbeaten club hosted the 1-2 New England Patriots in Week 4, and Drake Maye and company emerged with a 29-26 victory.
Since then, the defending AFC East champions own a 3-2 mark, while the Bills are on a four-game roll . At 7-1, the franchise is off to its best start since their fourth and last Super Bowl season of 1993. The club finished 12-4 but eventual fell to the Dallas Cowboys in Atlanta, 30-13, in Super Bowl XXVIII.
This week’s foe is the rival New York Jets , a team that the Bills have certainly handled in recent seasons. And it’s certainly a club that can’t be overlooked despite its 2-7 record.
Including a playoff win in 1981, the Bills own a big edge (73-58) in the all-time series standings. This decade, Buffalo has prevailed in 10 of the 12 meetings. The club has won the last five meetings by a combined 160-58 count.
A season ago, the Bills swept the Jets for the fourth time in six seasons. In Week 2 at MetLife Stadium, Josh Allen and company came up with a 30-10 victory. James Cook ran for 132 yards and two scores, part of a 224-yard rushing day by Buffalo.
Four months later at Orchard Park (Week 18), Allen (1) and Cook (2) combined for three offensive plays before giving way to Mitch Trubisky and Ray Davis. The former threw four touchdown passes, while Davis ran for 151 yards in the team’s 35-8 victory.
Minkah Fitzpatrick gives the Jets their first INT in 636 pass attempts NYJvsCHI on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/CQUCl4JVnt
The Bills gave up the fifth-most rushing yards in the league a year ago. Under new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard, the team has made significant strides in this area. Buffalo has limited its last four foes to under 80 yards rushing, this after giving up 116.0 yards per game on the ground in its first four outings.
Dating back to the start of 2025, Aaron Glenn’s team has picked off one pass in 26 games. A year ago, the team set dubious NFL single-season marks with zero interceptions and four total takeaways. This season, the Jets have forced a respectable 10 turnovers. They lead the NFL with nine opponent fumble recoveries.

On Tuesday, Bills’ GM Brandon Beane sent a second-round pick in 2027 to the Tennessee Titans and got back the NFL’s co-interception leader and a fifth-round selection next year. Seven-year pro Amani Hooker has picked off five passes in 2026. Buffalo has totaled only six interceptions in eight games this season.
New York’s defense is ranked a pretty respectable 12th in the league in fewest total yards allowed per game. But only six team in the leagues are giving up more yards per contest (128.0 average) on the ground. Joe Brady’s club is running for an impressive 146.6 yards per game, second-best in the NFL.

title: Why Did Bills Elevate QB Shane Buechele in Week 10? Is Josh Allen Okay to Face Jets?
full_text:
Breathe easy, Buffalo Bills ' fans.
Quarterback Josh Allen is not injured, and he's still scheduled to start against the New York Jets in The Meadowlands on Sunday.
While Allen, a five-time NFL MVP finalist, and backup QB Kyle Allen are both expected to be fully available for the 1 p.m. ET kickoff on November 15, the Bills elected to expend a gameday elevation on practice squad quarterback Shane Buechele.
In addition to the lone call-up, Buffalo made a roster swap out in its defensive secondary on Saturday. The Bills activated defensive back Jordan Hancock from Injured Reserve, and released Te'Cory Couch in a corresponding move that opened a roster spot for the former.
As a result of the elevation, Buechele is eligible to dress for the divisional road test against the Jets. Furthermore, the Bills aren't required to use a gameday roster spot for him.
Buffalo is likely to list Buechele amongst the Week 10 inactives while designating him as the emergency third quarterback. In that case, he can only enter the game in the nightmare scenario where both Allens suffer injuries.
Likely less concerned about having an emergency QB option available, the Bills have presumably made this move as a courtesy to Buechele for his work thus far this season. It also allows him to earn an active roster game check, which is significantly higher than his weekly practice squad pay.
Buechele is considered a valuable voice in the Bills' quarterbacks room, and he's seemingly developed a fantastic working relationship with Allen.
The 28-year-old Buechele initially joined the Bills' practice squad after being released by the Kansas City Chiefs following training camp in 2022.
Buffalo has kept the undrafted Buechele as its third quarterback for a fourth straight season. Although he has yet to appear in a regular season game for the Bills, he made his NFL debut in Week 18 last year after being claimed off the practice squad by the Chiefs .
After the 2025 regular season finale, Kansas City cut Buechele loose, and he subsequently rejoined the Bills for the playoffs.
Buechele performed adequately over the course of three preseason games this past summer, but he ultimately finished behind Kyle Allen in the QB2 competition.

title: Ex-Bills Safety CJ Gardner-Johnson Finally Speaks After Release, Blames Everyone Else
full_text:
This past offseason, the Buffalo Bills rolled the dice on C.J. Gardner-Johnson, a talented player who has worn out his welcome at multiple stops.
In 2025, Gardner-Johnson played for three different teams, after being released by the Houston Texans after just three games. He spent time on the Baltimore Ravens practice squad before finishing the season with the Chicago Bears.
This year, he lasted just six games with the Bills and was released following a one-game suspension for spitting at Brock Bowers. Nearly two weeks after being let go, Gardner-Johnson is finally speaking out and it's clear he learned very little from his latest setback.
Not only did Gardner-Johnson refuse to own up to his failures in Buffalo , but he also decided to point the finger. He claimed everyone turned on him while wildly claiming he didn't get the same opportunities other players received.
"In just a couple weeks, EVERYONE turned on me! No friends, no real support, it sucks we live in a society where one move can cause a downfall to anything! If this the last time y'all see my face or hear from me it’s cause you don’t understand the person, went through years of pain, alone, suffering trying to fit in, never got the same opportunity everybody else got!"
"And when I say same opportunities, just check my history “my attitude and character” my position but no real stories to back that up! It’s ok though as a man I just pray that one day it get better," Gardner-Johnson wrote on his social media accounts .
While we never want to see anyone struggling through any type of pain, it's hard to read this and find much sympathy for Gardner-Johnson. He claims that he is being held back because teams are focused on his "attitude and character," but those questions arose from his own actions.
It's also wild to hear the claim that he doesn't get the same opportunities when he has had three different homes since the Texans moved on last year. He just hasn't capitalized on those chances.
One of the primary reasons was his refusal to take accountability. Gardner-Johnson never admitted to spitting at Bowers , instead making the absurd claim that he was simply being competitive. That lack of accountability is exactly why the Bills were right to move on. His latest statement only reinforces that the veteran safety refuses to look in the mirror while giving Buffalo even more reason to believe they made the right call in saying goodbye.

title: Bills Make Defensive Back Roster Swap Prior to Visiting Jets for Division Game
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills are welcoming Jordan Hancock back to action.
Activating the versatile defensive back off Injured Reserve on Saturday, the Bills made him eligible to face the New York Jets in Week 10.
In order to make room for Hancock on the 53-man roster, Buffalo released defensive back Te'Cory Couch in a corresponding transaction. Couch appeared in four games for the Bills already this season, two as a practice squad call-up and two after signing to the roster on October 31 amidst Chauncey Gardner-Johnson's one-game suspension for spitting.
Couch played 36 defensive snaps, and made five tackles, in the 36-10 win over the Baltimore Ravens on November 1. In the other three appearances, however, he was used strictly as a special teamer.
With room for one more on their practice squad, the Bills seem likely to bring Couch back into the building come Tuesday. Being that the NFL trade deadline has passed, however, he'll be required to go through waivers before potentially rejoining Buffalo.
Hancock, a 2025 fifth-round draft pick, last saw the field in Week 2 against the Detroit Lions on Thursday Night Football. He logged 13 defensive snaps in that game as a nickel cornerback.
Interestingly enough, Hancock was on the injury report heading into that September 17 tilt due to a quad issue. He was a full participant throughout the practice week, and cleared for the game.
In Week 3, Hancock showed up on the Wednesday practice report as limited due to a hamstring. He was absent on that Thursday and Friday, suggesting that the injury occurred at some point during Wednesday's work at One Bills Drive.
Buffalo wasted no time placing Hancock on IR that Friday prior to the September 27 game against the Los Angeles Chargers. He remained on the shelf until the Bills officially opened his 21-day activation window and welcomed him back to practice on November 5.
As a rookie, Hancock switched positions to safety under prior head coach Sean McDermott.
With new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard taking over this year, the Bills moved Hancock back into more of a cornerback role , backing up slot corner Dee Alford and seeing time as an extra defensive back in some formations.
"He's done a great job. Obviously, in the game, he flashed his playmaking ability as well and his physicality. He plays fast. He plays violent. You're seeing more consistency the more reps he gets," said Leonhard following the Bills preseason opener.
Despite being sidelined during the offseason program due to injury, Hancock has shown little difficulty fitting into the system.
"When he's on the football field, you notice him. He flies around. He makes plays. He looks like he has fun playing football. He's a chess piece for us," said Bills' head coach Joe Brady in mid-August.
Fittingly, Hancock's return comes as the Bills prepare for a Jets team that has returned to full strength at wide receiver .

title: Bills' New-Look Secondary Won't Catch Break After Latest Jets Injury Updates
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills' defense has caught some breaks over the last few weeks thanks to injuries their opponents have dealt with, which has been welcomed for Buffalo's struggling defense.
In Week 8, the Bills avoided not only Lamar Jackson but also Tyler Huntley after both Baltimore Ravens quarterbacks exited the contest early due to injury.
Then, in Week 9, the Bills had the pleasure of facing Carson Wentz, who threw up an all-time stinker in Buffalo's 23-6 win over the Minnesota Vikings.
It looked like the Bills' new-look secondary that now features trade deadline acquisition Amani Hooker might catch another break in Week 10 because all three of the New York Jets' top wideouts were dealing with injuries, but it turns out that won't happen.
According to CBS Sports' Matt Zenitz , Jets wide receivers Garrett Wilson, Adonai Mitchell and Omar Cooper Jr. are all expected to play on Sunday afternoon.
Wilson was ruled out last week because of a concussion, but he was able to log a full practice on Friday , which was the first sign Wilson was going to play.
Cooper was a new addition to the injury report this week with an ankle issue, but just like Wilson he closed out his week with a full practice, signaling the rookie would go.
Mitchell was a late addition to the injury report during the week after popping up with a knee injury on Friday, but he also fully participated, so there wasn't much concern.
While we don't normally think of the Jets' offense as being any kind of test, that is certainly the case this year and nobody should underestimate their wide receiver trio that has a quarterback in Geno Smith who can get them the football consistently.
Wilson has been one of the more underrated wide receivers in the league during his career and the only reason he doesn't get more recognition is because he has routinely been stuck on terrible offenses, which has impacted his production.
After it looked like Mitchell would be a complete bust as a former second-round pick of the Indianapolis Colts, Mitchell has found new life with the Jets and is proving to be a viable deep threat.
Meanwhile, Cooper has wasted no time making an impact in his rookie season, with the Indiana product notching a pair of 100-yard games over the five contests he has played in.
Wilson, Cooper and Mitchell provide threats at all three areas of the field. Wilson can make plays all over, Cooper is great after the catch from the short-to-intermediate areas of the field, and as we mentioned with Mitchell, he can make plays down the field.
The Bills enter this game with the fourth-worst pass defense in the NFL, and they have given up a whopping 28 completions of 20-plus yards.
This is where Hooker comes into play. The former Titans safety is at his best in the deep part of the field , where his awareness and coverage ability should help improve what has been a major problem for defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard's unit.
According to Pro Football Focus , Hooker's 75.2 coverage grade ranks 11th among safeties, and he has five picks, which is four more than Bills safeties have combined.
We know Smith has a propensity to turn the football over, so don't be surprised if Hooker comes away with a pick in his first game with the Bills.

title: Grading Bills' 2026 Free Agency Additions at Midseason
full_text:
General manager Brandon Beane made a big move for the Buffalo Bills at the NFL trade deadline, adding safety Amani Hooker in a trade with the Tennessee Titans. That fills arguably their biggest need, but it's not the only thing Beane did to try and fix this roster.
During the offseason, they traded for wide receiver DJ Moore to shore up their receiving corps. Buffalo was also active in free agency, with names such as Bradley Chubb standing out as their top signing.
Now that we are approaching the midway point in the season, let's take a look at the players signed in free agency and assign a grade for each move.
Signing CJ Gardner-Johnson to a one-year deal was always a gamble. Gardner-Johnson has the talent to be a difference-maker in the secondary, but he has worn out his welcome in a hurry at multiple stops.
That proved to be the case again in 2026 as he was suspended for spitting at Brock Bowers in Week 6. Gardner-Johnson took no real accountability for his actions and after serving his suspension, the Bills released him. Buffalo had to eat his $3.5 million salary , which isn't a ton in the grand scheme of things, but this was a signing that failed.
This signing hardly made any noise, but the Bills did well by bringing in Greg Gaines on a $1.5 million deal just ahead of the regular season. Gaines was added to do "the dirty work," meaning he wouldn't rack up stats. That's held true, with Gaines recording just 11 tackles. That said, he has an overall PFF grade of 63.9 which is 45th out of 126 qualified defensive tackles. He's been strong against the run, earning a 62.5, which is the 37th best. That's solid work from a player on a minimal salary, which makes this a good move from Beane.
Buffalo decided to move on from Taron Johnson after a rough 2025 campaign and replaced him with Dee Alford. The former Falcon signed a three-year, $15.75 million contract, which can increase to $21 million with incentives.
Alford enters Week 10 with 19 tackles, three pass defenses, and one interception. He hasn't made a huge impact and has surrendered 16 receptions while giving up 14.4 yards per reception . The move hasn't been terrible, but it hasn't produced the results Beane hoped for.
Speaking of not producing the results expected, Bradley Chubb hasn't lived up to his contract through his first nine weeks in Buffalo. Chubb signed a three-year, $43.5 million deal with the belief that he could give them a solid pass-rushing presence opposite Greg Rousseau.
Through eight games, Chubb has 18 tackles and 1.5 sacks. His lack of production has Bills On SI's John Green naming him the team's biggest disappointment . It's hard to argue against that, although there's still time for Chubb to catch fire.

title: Bills Trade Rumors From ESPN Name Star DT Among 4 Players Buffalo Aggressively Pursued
full_text:
As we put the NFL trade deadline further and further behind us, more and more details are emerging about the Buffalo Bills' pursuits.
Of course, the Bills came away with a big trade before the deadline passed thanks to the acquisition of safety Amani Hooker and a fifth-round pick from the Tennessee Titans in exchange for a second-round selection.
But he was just one of four players the Bills pursued ahead of the trade deadline, and they weren't only after a safety, either.
According to ESPN's Ian Rapoport and Adam Schefter , the Bills were among the "two teams that were most aggressive" in talks with the Philadelphia Eagles for star defensive tackle Jordan Davis, who ultimately landed with the Jacksonville Jaguars.
"The two teams that were most aggressive in trading for Eagles defensive tackle Jordan Davis were the Bills and Jaguars, who wound up trading a first- and second-round pick to the Eagles," Schefter and Rapoport wrote.
While there was some speculation about the Bills possibly adding another defensive tackle, it's not like that was a dire need with Ed Oliver and Deone Walker upfront. If anything, we anticipated a smaller move than what acquiring Davis would have been.
Adding Davis would have given Buffalo an embarrassment of riches along the defensive line, as Davis is one of the better players at his position in the NFL.
Spending that much on another defensive tackle when it wasn't a huge need likely would have drawn criticism for general manager Brandon Beane, who won a lot of favor with the Hooker trade .
According to Schefter and Rapoport, the Bills were after two other safeties besides Hooker.
Those safeties were Budda Baker of the Arizona Cardinals and Jessie Bates, who was traded to the Jaguars from the Atlanta Falcons.
"The two teams most aggressive for former Falcons safety Jessie Bates also were the Bills and Jaguars, who traded second- and fifth-round picks to Atlanta," the ESPN reporters said.
After missing out on Bates, the Bills turned their focus to Hooker and Baker, but the Cardinals were unwilling to trade him.
"After the Jaguars traded for Davis and Bates, the Bills pivoted to two safeties: Arizona's Budda Baker and Tennessee's Amani Hooker," they added.
"The Cardinals declined to trade their respected veteran safety, but the Titans listened and agreed to trade Hooker and a fifth-round pick to the Bills for a second-round pick."
Baker and Bates would have been welcomed additions, no doubt, but we tend to believe Hooker was the best fit for the Bills — and for a few reasons.
Hooker is better in coverage than Baker, as evidenced by the former's Pro Football Focus coverage grade being nearly 27 points higher.
That's important to note because the Bills' biggest weakness on defense has been the pass defense, which is the fourth-worst in the NFL. The Bills have also had issues letting up explosive plays, with defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard's unit giving up 28 over eight contests.
Bates has posted a better PFF coverage grade than Hooker this season, but he is also in the final year of his deal, so the Bills would have been giving up significant draft capital for a player who may not be back in 2027.
Meanwhile, Hooker, who came cheaper, is locked up through 2028 and has outs in his deal in each of the next two years if things don't pan out, and he's a full year younger than Bates, also.
Hooker may not have been the Bills' top target, nor is he the most accomplished between the three safeties, but he still amounts to one heck of a consolation prize.
