title: Saints Injury Report: Tyler Shough Loses Two Key Protectors Against Panthers
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints will be short-handed in Sunday’s rivalry game with the Carolina Panthers , with the heaviest hits being on the offensive line.
Head coach Kellen Moore ruled out multiple players with injuries, including two starting offensive linemen: center Erik McCoy (bicep) and right tackle Taliese Fuaga (knee). The team will also miss rookie running back CJ Donaldson (shoulder) and second-round defensive lineman Christen Miller (knee).
The Saints got a little more than three quarters of football out of their starting five offensive linemen last week before McCoy exited with an injury. Then Fuaga suffered a knee sprain in practice. Moore said Fuaga isn’t expected to miss enough time to land on injured reserve, but McCoy’s outlook is less certain.
A few other players are questionable for Sunday’s game with the Carolina Panthers. Running back Travis Etienne Jr. (hamstring) is the big name, but cornerback Martin Emerson Jr. is one to watch, too. We’ll find out for sure when the inactives list is published on Sunday.
The Saints got more than three quarters of action from their starting offensive line in last week's win over the Cleveland Browns before McCoy exited with a biceps injury.
The situation worsened when Fuaga suffered a knee sprain during practice, leaving New Orleans without two important pieces of its offensive front.
Moore indicated Fuaga's injury is not expected to require a stint on injured reserve, although McCoy's recovery timeline remains uncertain.
McCoy's absence could prove particularly challenging as he plays a critical role in identifying defensive fronts, communicating protection adjustments and helping maintain continuity across the offensive line as the center.
Without him, New Orleans must rely on Cesar Ruiz to handle those responsibilities while adjusting to a reshuffled interior with Jeremiah Wright taking Ruiz’s spot at right guard.
Fuaga's injury creates another significant concern at right tackle, where Asim Richards could be called upon to step into the starting lineup.
The Saints also dealt with injuries involving left tackle Kelvin Banks Jr. (ankle) and guard David Edwards (knee) throughout the week. While both returned to full participation Friday, it’s another sign that this unit is not even close to 100%.
Even with Banks and Edwards, losing two starters makes it hard for an offensive line that has struggled with pass protection and consistency in the running game.

title: Saints Stock Up: Audric Estimé Makes a Statement, Pass Rush Keeps Rolling
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints gave their home crowd reason to celebrate on Sunday at Caesars Superdome, clinching a thrilling 23-22 victory in overtime over the Cleveland Browns .
While improving the Saints to 3-5 and snapping a home slump, the win was far from flawless.
The result grants head coach Kellen Moore a brief reprieve, but ongoing flaws demonstrate that his standing stays uncertain.
With a tough slate ahead, New Orleans needs to fix key errors to sustain progress.
Below are the Saints players and units whose stock rose after Sunday's thrilling finish.
Despite rejoining the Saints via waivers after getting cut after training camp, running back Audric Estimé made a compelling argument for an expanded role in New Orleans' backfield despite being back in New Orleans for a week.
The second-year running back rushed for 72 yards and a touchdown on 15 carries, averaging 4.8 yards per attempt.
His biggest contribution came late in regulation when he powered into the end zone from 2 yards out to give New Orleans a 16-13 advantage.
Beyond the touchdown, Estimé provided the physicality and downhill running that the Saints have struggled to establish consistently.
Charlie Smyth made the most of his opportunity after he became the starter after the Saints released Daniel Carlson .
The Irish-born kicker connected on three of his four field-goal attempts against Cleveland, converting from 30, 27 and 48 yards.
With both offenses struggling to finish drives, Smyth accounted for all nine of New Orleans' points through the first three quarters.
His 48-yard field goal in the fourth quarter briefly gave the Saints a 9-6 advantage.
The Saints' pass rush continues to emerge as one of the team's biggest strengths, with Carl Granderson and Chase Young leading a pass rush that made life miserable for Cleveland quarterback Shedeur Sanders .
Granderson recorded two sacks against the Browns, extending his streak of games with multiple sacks to four. According to the Saints, he became the first NFL player since 2013 to accomplish that feat.
Young added his eighth sack of the season, while Kaden Elliss and Khristian Boyd also got into the action as New Orleans finished with five sacks.
The Saints' defensive front also made its presence felt against the run, limiting Cleveland to 95 rushing yards while consistently disrupting the Browns' offensive rhythm.
Perhaps the unit's most impressive moment came near the goal line, when New Orleans delivered a critical fourth-down stand to keep Cleveland out of the end zone.
Although the Saints' secondary remains vulnerable to explosive plays, the defensive front has become a reliable source of pressure and physicality.

title: Saints Trading DL Godchaux to Jaguars Signals Continued Youth Movement on Defense
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints are finalizing a trade that will send veteran defensive tackle Davon Godchaux to the Jacksonville Jaguars , another move signaling the organization's willingness to prioritize its future over veteran experience.
NFL insider Jordan Schultz reported that New Orleans will receive a 2028 sixth-round draft pick that could become a 2027 sixth-round pick if Jacksonville acquires one through a trade or the compensatory process.
The deal comes just one day after the Saints secured a thrilling 23-22 overtime win over the Cleveland Browns , improving to 3-5.
While the trade provides New Orleans with additional draft capital, it offers little immediate financial relief.
For salary cap reasons, the Saints had restructured Godchaux's contract by converting the bulk of his pay into a signing bonus, leaving only $650,000 of his $1.3 million base salary.
As Godchaux turns 32 this week and approaches the final year of his deal, he became an expendable veteran for a team placing greater emphasis on nurturing younger talent.
New Orleans initially acquired the Plaquemine, Louisiana native from the New England Patriots in March 2025, surrendering a 2026 seventh-round pick while assuming the remaining two years and $11 million of his contract following a restructuring.
Although Godchaux appeared in all eight games this season, his role has gotten smaller and smaller by the week. Godchaux started the first five games, but hehas  played just eight, 18 and 12 defensive snaps over the last three games.
However, Godchaux still contributed to one of the Saints' biggest defensive plays Sunday, helping stop Cleveland on a critical fourth-and-goal opportunity.
The departure of Godchaux opens up substantial playing time for the Saints' younger defensive linemen, most notably Khristian Boyd and rookie second-round selection Christen Miller .
Boyd, who recorded a sack and a tackle for loss Sunday and played a key role alongside Godchaux in the goal-line stand, is expected to see an expanded workload at center of New Orleans' defensive line.
At the same time, accelerating Miller's progress becomes more urgent, especially since the rookie was a healthy scratch for the matchup against Cleveland.
Ultimately, this deal signifies more for New Orleans than just swapping a veteran player for late-round draft compensation.
It reflects a clear strategic shift by the front office to assess its youth roster while continuing to stockpile future draft assets.
How well New Orleans fills the void left by Godchaux upfront will largely hinge on whether Boyd and Miller can take full advantage of their new opportunities.

title: The Good, Bad and Ugly From Saints' Wild Overtime Win Over Browns
full_text:
The New Orleans Saints finally gave their home crowd something to celebrate Sunday, securing a thrilling 23-22 overtime victory over the Cleveland Browns at Caesars Superdome.
But while the Saints improved to 3-5 and snapped their home winless streak, the victory was far from pretty.
For Kellen Moore , the victory provided some much-needed relief, but it also exposed several problems that continue to plague his team and will keep him on the hot seat.
With a difficult stretch of the schedule ahead, the Saints have plenty to clean up if they want to build momentum.
Here’s a look at the good, the bad and the ugly from New Orleans' dramatic overtime victory over Cleveland.
Tyler Shough continues to show his clutch gene, even if the organization he plays for is in shambles.
Shough completed 21 of 35 passes for 265 yards and a touchdown while adding 51 rushing yards on 10 carries. While he didn’t do much for most of the game, it’s when his team needed him the most he stepped up. His composure in critical situations stood out.
Trailing 13-9 late in the fourth quarter, Shough orchestrated a 55-yard touchdown drive in just 50 seconds, highlighted by a 33-yard completion to Chris Olave that set up Audric Estimé 's 2-yard touchdown run.
After Cleveland forced overtime, Shough responded again, leading an 11-play, 74-yard touchdown drive capped by a perfectly placed 15-yard pass to ever-reliable tight end Juwan Johnson . That drive was his fifth game-winning drive of the season.
The performance was particularly encouraging, given that Shough was sacked five times and played late in the game without starting center Erik McCoy .
Estimé also provided an unexpected spark, rushing for 72 yards and a touchdown on 15 carries just days after being claimed off waivers.
Despite scoring 23 points, the New Orleans Saints ' offense struggled again.
The Saints didn't score a touchdown until Estimé’s run with 58 seconds remaining, settling for field goals despite moving the ball effectively at times. The Saints also only converted on two of their five red zone opportunities.
Their struggles were particularly evident in the first half, when New Orleans outgained Cleveland 176-80 but entered halftime tied 3-3.
The offensive line also had its share of problems, surrendering five sacks and repeatedly forcing Shough to escape pressure.
Even with left tackle Kelvin Banks Jr. back, the Saints struggled to protect their quarterback consistently.
Sure, several individuals had encouraging performances, but New Orleans still lacks inspiration on offense and the ability to put opponents away.
Without starting quarterback Deshaun Watson , the Saints had multiple chances to take control against Cleveland but instead needed late-game heroics.
The Saints won't always be fortunate enough to overcome those shortcomings. The Carolina Panthers are up next, but the following three games: two road games back-to-back against the Chicago Bears and the Cincinnati Bengals and a home matchup against the Green Bay Packers .
If there's one area that should frustrate Kellen Moore more than anything else, it's the Saints' inability to protect the football.
New Orleans committed two costly second-quarter turnovers, both involving rookies, that completely changed the complexion of the game.
First-round pick Jordyn Tyson , making his NFL debut after missing the first seven games with a hamstring injury, fumbled near Cleveland's goal line moments after making his first career reception on the same play.
The turnover wasted a promising scoring opportunity after Shough connected with Barion Brown for a 52-yard gain.
Things somehow got worse moments later.
After the defense forced a punt, Brown fumbled the return, giving Cleveland possession at the Saints' 19-yard line.
Fortunately for New Orleans, the defense bailed out the offense and special teams, stopping Quinshon Judkins on fourth-and-goal from the 1-yard line.
But the mistakes weren't limited to turnovers.
The Saints' defense also surrendered a 64-yard touchdown pass from Shedeur Sanders to KC Concepcion Jr. immediately after taking a 9-6 lead in the fourth quarter.
Then, after Estimé put New Orleans ahead with 58 seconds remaining, the defense allowed Cleveland to move into position for a game-tying 51-yard field goal.
And even after Shough delivered an overtime touchdown, the Saints surrendered a 39-yard touchdown reception to Harold Fannin Jr. , forcing the defense to make one final stand.
New Orleans escaped with a victory, but the combination of turnovers, blown coverage and late defensive breakdowns nearly turned a much-needed win into another devastating loss.

title: Giants’ Sneak Over Tush Push Call Remains a Head-Scratcher
full_text:
Most New York Giants fans agree that the team’s decision to run a quarterback sneak on a 3rd-and-1 rather than a classic tush push in its 24-21 loss to the Washington Commanders was a head-scratcher.
And apparently, if the stats are to be believed, the questions are justified. According to TushPush.fyi , the Giants have run three tush push plays this season, all of which were successful.
What about quarterback sneaks? Per PFF’s advanced data , quarterback Jameis Winston ranks fourth among quarterbacks with 11 sneaks, and his eight first downs on sneaks also rank fourth in the league.
Given the success of the tush push, then, why not go for that play on 3rd-and-short rather than a sneak?
There are a couple of potential reasons. The first, as head coach John Harbaugh noted to the media on Friday, is that the offensive line did a much better job run-blocking against a banged-up Washington defensive front.
While Harbaugh didn’t say much, perhaps offensive coordinator Matt Nagy felt more confident calling for a sneak than a tush push, given how the offensive line was blocking.
Statistically, the Giants averaged 4.3 yards per rush attempt against Washington, with two rushing touchdowns in the loss. Against the Eagles, they struggled to run the ball, averaging 2.6 yards per carry without Cam Skattebo, who was inactive.
In addition, against the Eagles, the Giants had eight rushing attempts that went for zero or negative yards. Against Washington, they had only two such unsuccessful attempts.
Along those lines, the Giants averaged 4.16 yards per attempt on rushes between the tackles in the loss to Washington. In contrast, against Philadelphia, they averaged 2.2 yards per attempt between the tackles.
All that being said, the question of how they decide between a sneak and a tush push is the one Harbaugh sidestepped when it was put to him on Friday.
“We have four or five of those different types of calls and motions and pushes—not pushes, check-with-me plays. There are different things that we have. One of those was called,” he said.
“We have different calls that go with quarterback sneaks, so we didn’t call the same one that we’ve been calling. That’s really the only answer I have for you.”
The other unanswered question is whether Winston checked out of a play. Asked about the 3rd-and-1 on which Skattebo stayed in the backfield for almost two seconds, Harbaugh clarified that the play “was a normal quarterback sneak and a certain check involved in it that is part of the play.”
The bottom line is that the play, regardless of what was called versus what was executed, failed to convert. It could be one that Nagy wishes he had back, and he will almost certainly be asked about it the next time the coordinators speak with the media on Thursday.
That play itself isn’t why the Giants lost, but it added to a night of frustration for fans who were expecting a Big Blue win in a critical divisional game.

title: The Inches That Are Affecting Giants’ Rookie Kicker Dominic Zvada's FGAs
full_text:
The New York Giants head coach is not ready to give up on rookie placekicker Dominic Zvada despite the former Michigan kicker’s inconsistencies over the last few weeks, which have seen him go 8-for-14 after making his first nine field-goal attempts.
Zvada’s recent woes have come from the right hash, including his lone 33-yard field goal attempt that sailed wide left in the Giants’ 24-21 loss to the Washington Commanders on Thursday night. That 33-yard miss was his first under 40 yards this season.
“There’s a technique issue there with his plant foot that we’re kind of looking at,” head coach John Harbaugh said on Friday. “And he needs to clean that up from a consistency standpoint. He knows that. Popped up again in that one kick there. I had a chance to watch it this morning. There is an issue on the right hash, no question.”
Harbaugh didn’t go into detail on what the issue is with Zvada’s plant foot, but according to retired Giants kicker Lawrence Tynes, the issue may be that Zvada’s plant foot is too deep and close to the ball.
Tynes, in a social media post on Oct. 14 referencing one of the rookie’s misses from the right hash, said Zvada’s plant foot is “too deep and close to the ball.”
He added, “Out in front and close to the ball can cause you to hook or push it.”
One on left is a make. Ankle in plant leg is lined up with the ball. This is good. One on the right is a miss. Plant foot is too deep and close to the ball. Out in front and close to the ball can cause you to hook or push it. Not good. Can be caused by trying to go too hard… pic.twitter.com/q6diGyURZL
Tynes further explained that Zvada’s issue in front of the ball can be caused by trying to go too hard at the ball to create power on longer kicks. “You get too deep and close with the plant. We are talking about inches here.”
Assistant head coach and special teams coordinator Chris Horton told reporters last month, after Zvada’s struggles on Washington’s wet grass field, that the playing surface can also affect a young kicker’s effectiveness.
“Footing is definitely a lot different,” he said. “Obviously, the turf, your plant foot sticks a little bit; it sticks a little bit better. When you’re on grass and things like that, your foot might slide a little bit more.”
Tynes, who called himself “a huge fan” of Zvada’s, endorses the patient approach Harbaugh and the Giants are taking, despite any frustration over the lost points.
“He is an elite talent learning how to become a consistent NFL kicker,” Tynes told New York Giants On SI .
“His leg talent does not grow on trees. He has more talent in his pinky toe than I ever had. Patience is required.”

title: Giants 2027 NFL Draft Watch: Four College Prospects to Track This Weekend
full_text:
As the New York Giants (5-3-1) absorb their 24-21 Week 10 loss to the Washington Commanders on Thursday Night Football at MetLife Stadium, several Big Blue scouts will be watching closely. College football’s Week 11 slate is about to unfold.
While several potential targets make their case for being selected in the 2027 NFL Draft, the team’s biggest needs are becoming clearer.
In addition to their most pressing need at defensive tackle, coach John Harbaugh and his staff may also want to add players who can bolster their depth charts on offense and on special teams.
Here are four players the Giants may be keeping an eye on this weekend.
Gilliam is rapidly becoming one of the nation’s most fearsome defensive tackles, as evidenced by his rising draft stock.
The 6-foot-2, 305-pound lineman has amassed 26 total tackles, six sacks and two forced fumbles in nine games this season with the Volunteers.
His ability to hold his position against the run, combined with his elite first step when rushing the passer, should make him an immediate upgrade on any NFL defensive line he joins in 2027.
Because he projects best as a three-technique in a 4-3 scheme, Gilliam may not be the big, two-gap tackle the Giants are expected to pursue during the draft.
However, he could be an effective weapon in sub-packages within the Giants’ 3-4 defense, especially when the unit shifts into four-man nickel fronts on passing downs.
With Tennessee set for a marquee matchup against Texas A&M, Gilliam is expected to play a major role in disrupting the Aggies’ offense, led by quarterback Marcel Reed.
Should the Giants prioritize power when scouting potential interior offensive linemen, Knapp is likely to be among their top prospects. The Roswell, Ga., native has appeared in eight games this season at left guard for the Fighting Irish.
With experience in both zone and gap schemes, the Notre Dame product appears ready to make an impact in any pro-level offensive system.
With the Irish set to face Boston College’s aggressive defense, Knapp will be called upon to remain a reliable presence in both pass protection and run-blocking alignments.
With John Michael Schmitz likely heading to free agency after being replaced in the starting lineup by Bryan Hudson, the 6-foot-4, 305-pound Knapp could be an intriguing option for New York, with the versatility to play either guard or center.
While Brown may not be the three-down workhorse New York reportedly coveted at the trade deadline, his skill set could be an intriguing fit within their current stable of running backs.
At 5-foot-9 and 190 pounds, Brown is a bit on the lighter side to handle lead-back duties at the pro level. Still, he could be an impactful change-of-pace option or an effective pass-catcher out of the backfield.
If the Giants show interest in Brown, it may be to pair him with Cam Skattebo.
With Skattebo as their physical, between-the-tackles runner atop the depth chart, Louisville’s standout could add an explosive dynamic to New York’s backfield.
If he’s effective against North Carolina’s defense under coach Bill Belichick, Brown may force the Giants to take a good look at him come draft time.
Given rookie Dominic Zvada’s continued struggles, the Giants have been the subject of rumors at kicker. Fortunately for Big Blue, several college kickers could draw interest, including Woodring.
In nine games for the top-ranked Bulldogs this season, Woodring has made 9 of 13 field goals, with his longest coming from 49 yards. He has also made a perfect 47 of 47 extra-point attempts. In 2025, Woodring connected on 17 of 19 field goals (89.5%), with a long of 53.
Despite his struggles this season, including a 49-yard miss against Ole Miss in Week 10, Woodring has the power and consistency to be a reliable kicker in his rookie season. While the Giants have expressed their support for Zvada, they are likely keeping their options open.
If Woodring can score points on Saturday against Missouri, it may help improve his draft stock with positionally needy teams like the Giants.

title: Why Cam Skattebo Stayed Put on Giants’ Key Third-and-1 Against Commanders
full_text:
To the casual observer, New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo looked like he had fallen asleep at the snap, staying in his stance for nearly two seconds on a third-and-1 rushing play by quarterback Jameis Winston that did not pick up the first down.
But the play, which many assumed was a tush push given how often the Giants have run it this year, wasn’t what it looked like, and Skattebo did what he was supposed to do.
“That wasn’t a tush push. That was a different kind of play,” head coach John Harbaugh explained.
“It was a normal quarterback sneak and a certain check involved in it that is part of the play, but it wasn’t a tush push. So (Skattebo) wasn’t supposed to be up there pushing.”
Weirdest play of a weird night. If you’re going to run the Tush Push, you have to … you know … push. 🤷🏻‍♂️ pic.twitter.com/Sf65ZJ1vrF
The play occurred with the Giants leading 21-17. After a third-down try that initially appeared to give Winston the first down before officials reversed the call, the Giants tried to draw the Commanders offside on fourth-and-1. Still, it didn’t work, and a delay of game penalty led to a punt.
Given the Giants' success with the tush push, it was surprising they didn’t bring extra bodies to help Winston get the first down.
The Giants have converted first downs on 43.5% of their quarterback rushing attempts, which is the fifth-best mark in the NFL.
While that stat doesn’t differentiate between tush pushes, sneaks, designed runs, and scrambles, it shows the Giants have succeeded when deploying their quarterbacks to do so.
Only Harbaugh and offensive coordinator Matt Nagy know the logic behind running a sneak over a tush push. Still, it raised eyebrows, given Skattebo’s late arrival to the play and the fact that fullback Patrick Ricard was also not involved in Winston’s attempt to move the chains.
“We have four or five of those different types of calls and motions and pushes, not pushes, check-with-me plays. There are different things we have. One of those was called,” Harbaugh explained.
“We have different calls that go with quarterback sneaks, so we didn’t call the same one that we’ve been calling. That’s really the only answer I have for you. We didn’t call the same play. He wasn’t supposed to be up there pushing.”
But with that call not resulting in a first-down conversion, questions will linger over whether it was the right call to make at that juncture.

title: Giants Mailbag: Malik Nabers, Kayvon Thibodeaux, and More
full_text:
Welcome to the weekly New York Giants On SI mailbag! From offseason moves to game-day strategies, we'll do our best to answer your questions. (Some questions have been edited for brevity and clarity.)
If Nabers fancies himself as one of the best in the league, he needs to play like it.  No more dropping touchdowns.  No more fumbling the ball.  No more temper tantrums.  Time for him to ascend.  Will anyone have an honest conversation with him?
Mike, I asked Nabers about that in a round about way. Here was his response: "I had a talk with (Quarterbacks) Coach (Brian) Callahan, and we had a good talk and he said some things in our conversation. He was just like, ‘Just play the one play that we call, don't try to do too much.’ Don't try to do a lot on the play, we just need you to be you. So just be you at the end of the day.
"And like I said, just not pressing. I'm getting a lot of different coverages on my side. I'm getting a lot of cloud, getting a lot of double teams. So, every opportunity I have to get the football I think I'm just trying to do too much with the football instead of just let the game come to me and just play the game. So, I think just like Coach Calli said, just playing that one play, just locking on that one play and then focus on the next play when it comes."
Now that the Giants did not trade Thibedeux what are the chances that he is resigned. Hopefully it will not be another Saqoun situation.
Moose, my gut says they don't re-sign Thibodeaux. He's going to want a top-dollar deal, and I think someone will give it to him.
I could see a world where Arvell Reese gets more snaps on the outside, and you also have to remember that Thibs has been playing in his natural spot ever since Brian Burns's season-ending injury. So I think Thibs moves on in free agency.
Why do you suppose o-line got away from pulling guards, and running trap plays like week one against Dallas. Seems like more straight up blocking to me now. Did Dart's injury force a change to the blocking scheme?
The injury to Dart may have had something to do with it — remember, they have only now run what, three games with J.J. McCarthy under center, a guy who can run the RPO game unlike Winston?  But I think the bigger issue was the injuries at running back.
First, you have Tyrone Tracy Jr. on IR, and of course you had Skattebo miss a game due to injury (as well as one due to a quasi-benching). As a result, the Giants leaned a little bit more on inside zone runs.
Second, I think they've leaned more on a pistol formation in their running game, with the fullback serving more as a trap blocker while the o-line has focused on DUO blocking.  The Giants only ran the pistol on 1.1% of their plays in Week 1.
Since then that perentage has jumped up to 3%, which might not seem like a huge jump but actually is considering how many rushing attempts they average per game.
What are the future ramifications to the Eagles salary cap since they are the biggest users of voidable years. How will it impact their rebuild.
Jim, I cover the Giants, not the Eagles so I can't sit here and tell you how their cap is going to be impacted down to the penny.
What I can tell you is that they have a lot of draft picks next year which means they'll have a lot of players on rookie deals -- two first rounders, one second, and a projected third round comp pick are their premium picks.
The cap is also going to rise so whatever dead money they accrue as a result of voidable years won't be as harsh in terms of the bite it takes out of their cap as it might be if it the hit were taken this year.
John Harbaugh says that Zavada has a problem on the right hash. Are you able to go back to see how many of his misses were from the right hash?
Kris, I was the one who mentioned Zvada's misses this year coming from the right hash, something Harbaugh didn't disagree with.
I brought up the question because I noticed they all came from the right hash. So to your question—I already did the groundwork on it, not that I was the only one to do so, I'm sure.

title: Giants Defense and Special Teams Grades: Safeties Shine, Kicking Game Falters
full_text:
You win some, you lose some.
But when you lose by death by a thousand paper cuts, as the New York Giants did in their 24-21 loss to the Washington Commanders on Thursday night, those are hard to swallow. That’s especially true when the loss came against a divisional opponent the Giants could have buried for the season and used to pad their lead in the NFC East.
“It’s a missed opportunity, but like I told the guys, it would have been great to win the game, but it doesn’t change our goals or our opportunity going forward,” head coach John Harbaugh said after the game.
“So, it’s a tough loss. It’s the National Football League. You’re going to lose some games. And everybody in this league is good. The Commanders are good. Everybody’s good. So, I mean, we have a really good team coming in here next Sunday [the Jacksonville Jaguars]. A team that we can beat, so we’ve just got to get back to work.”
That’s really all they can do, but let’s be frank: they could have used the win against Washington to carry some positive momentum into what is essentially the teeth of their schedule.
Four of the Giants’ next five opponents have winning records, and if the Giants’ goal is to get to the playoffs and make some noise, teams like those coming up over the next few weeks are what they will have to beat to prove they belong.
“We’ve got to find a way to get the next one. And the next one after that. And the next one after that. And get as many as we need to win the division. That’s what we’ve got to find a way to do. So trying to keep it in perspective is very important,” Harbaugh added.
It’s also probably easier said than done.
On that note, let’s look at what the film told us about the players on defense and special teams.
This big guy has spoiled us with his big-time nose tackle play so far this year, but he took a bit of a step back this week.
His lone tackle came on a splash play: a hustle tackle outside the box near the goal line that forced a third-and-goal.
The problem was that it came outside the box, where the defense needed Reader to be a bit more dominant between the tackles. The Commanders’ 105 yards on the ground were just enough to keep things two-dimensional.
Reader was physical as always, but he wasn’t finding the ball as well as he does. He seemed a bit sluggish and not as quick-thinking as he’s been.
Contributing again as the rotation nose tackle, Jamison-Travis finished with two tackles and regularly held his gap while also running to the edges when the ball went that way.
This kid stays on his feet most of the time. His pass-rushing remains nonexistent, but the life in his feet suggests there may be something to work with. The kid is getting plenty of serious snaps right now, and he’s holding up just fine.
Harris recorded his first sack of the year as the beneficiary of an Abdul Carter edge rush that attracted lots of attention.
Harris exploited the space by looping around the edge and then corralling the fleet-footed quarterback for the huge third-quarter sack.
Harris finished with four total tackles, including a quarterback hit and a tackle for loss. He seemed unusually fresh out there Thursday night.
Pitching in with his requisite one tackle, Alexander played exclusively on passing downs and showed a bit of buzz around the pocket, though with little finish.
His run defense continues to struggle, as he lacks the upper-body strength to shed a solo block. His strength is his lower-body agility, but he’s still not translating that talent into consistent production.
Getting another practice squad elevation, Smoot contributed much as he did last week with solid physical positional play and just enough mobility to chase in small places.
He finished with one assist while playing on his feet and absorbing power.
The fourth-and-goal pressure that Carter created should have been a bigger play, but the Commanders lucked out when the desperation heave into the end zone found an unwitting tight end’s hands for the score.
Carter did draw a fourth-quarter hold, but that was the extent of his pass-rush production. He faced some double teams, but nothing like last week, and he was unusually quiet again.
Washington also targeted his edge, as Carter was too often easily handled by solo blocking.
Double teams are neutralizing his explosiveness, and he isn’t making up for it with physicality. He’s got to find ways to fight through this attention, especially in big moments.
He finished with three total tackles, including a tackle for loss, but he needs more in his arsenal.
Thibodeaux’s eight total tackles this week were easily a season high, as he’s been picking up his play week by week and reached Thursday night’s level.
Most of his plays came against the run, either closing down from his edge or hustling to chase things down.
Several of his tackles came while chasing the quarterback out of bounds, and several more came while chasing down wide receivers.
Though he did produce a couple of decent pass rushes, he never got close to the end zone. He had no quarterback hits or tackles for loss on his sheet.
Getting a fair share of snaps at outside linebacker, Ford did a decent job holding his edge and chasing in pursuit, but he never found the ball.
Ford was hardly used in coverage this week, which had been his “thing” earlier in the year.
Leading the team with 13 total tackles, the rookie had none of last week’s big plays, though he did a fine job cleaning up things between the tackles using not only his raw physical ability but also his eyes.
His reads seem to be sharp and always under control. The Commanders did a good job recognizing Reese’s blitzes and neutralizing them, but he also spent most of those blitzes staying in front to contain the scrambling quarterback.
That strategy worked, as it forced Jayden Daniels to throw the ball late in the game and led to two interceptions, either one of which should have ended the game. Reese played a quietly effective game nonetheless despite the absence of flash plays.
Finishing second on the stat sheet with nine total tackles, McFadden was instrumental in stopping the occasional bleeding of the Washington run game with knifing attacks through the right gaps and stopping runs dead in their tracks.
He should have gotten credit for two tackles for loss, but the sheet shows only one.
McFadden was flagged for a fourth-quarter pass interference call when he rode a running back executing an out-and-up against him. He was slightly beaten, but not egregiously.
McFadden got credit for the biggest hit of the night on defense when he smacked Daniels on a fourth-quarter keeper, hitting him face up and stopping him dead in his tracks.
The team’s CB1 played another tight, forceful game, showing a couple of leaks but nothing egregious. Newsome’s tackle number on the sheet is usually significant since he’s such an aggressive hunter against the run.
He added four more tackles to his total, but very few passes targeted his area as the Commanders stayed away from him as much as possible.
Early on, Banks’ tight coverage on a slant forced a near-interception. He also managed three total tackles, including one in the backfield. But for every good play Banks makes, he also takes away.
As he did last week, Banks was targeted in a big moment. The opposition got a pass interference penalty that the officials couldn’t get out of their pockets fast enough, and the Commanders moved into their winning touchdown.
When Washington got the ball back at its own 29-yard line with 1:49 left in the fourth quarter, trailing by four, its first play was a deep shot right at Banks, who lost his man off the snap. The 33-yard penalty jump-started the drive.
It was an iffy call, but when Banks once again refused to look back for the ball, the resulting contact made the official’s job easy.
To make matters worse, on Washington’s game-winning catch-and-run touchdown, Banks had a legitimate chance to get in on the tackle, but instead he lollygagged around contact and…

title: Malik Nabers Reveals Advice He's Trying to Follow to Become a Better Player
full_text:
Malik Nabers wants to win more than anything, so much so that he beats himself up when he doesn’t do all he can to help the cause.
Such was the case for the New York Giants receiver, who had a game to forget in New York’s 24-21 loss to the Washington Commanders on Thursday night. He lost his first fumble of the season.
“Yeah, I mean, you’re thinking about plays that could have been a difference in the game, and that could have been one of those,” Nabers said of the fumble.
“We were in the red zone, could have got a field goal or a touchdown, and sadly went away just off a mistake that I made. But I mean, try to do better, try to be better, and I’ll be better at protecting the football, having awareness of where I am, and just like I said, protecting the football to give the offense opportunity to score points on that drive.”
Nabers, who explained that he left the postgame locker room to attend to a family emergency, finished the game with five receptions for 44 yards. He was also the intended target on the Commanders’ game-sealing interception by defensive back Rasul Douglas, a play on which Nabers has drawn criticism for not fighting to break it up.
“I mean, seeing the ball go up at the time, didn’t really see him or where he was,” he said about that play. “My head is looking up at the ball, even though he was driving on the ball. So, just seeing how high the ball was and just waiting for it to come down and made a jump to catch the ball and then got hit and then he made a play.”
Nabers tries not to let it show in public, but he takes his performance shortcomings and the losses that follow personally.
As a competitor, it’s easy for him to be swallowed up by those mishaps, but Nabers credited quarterbacks coach Brian Callahan for helping him keep his feet on the ground and not be consumed by things that happened in the past.
“We had a good talk, and he said some things in our conversation,” Nabers said of Callahan. “He was just like, ‘Just play the one play that we call, don’t try to do too much. Don’t try to do a lot on the play; we need you to be you. So just be you at the end of the day.’
“I’m getting a lot of different coverages on my side. I’m getting a lot of cloud, getting a lot of double teams. So, every opportunity I have to get the football, I think I’m just trying to do too much with the football instead of just letting the game come to me and play the game.”
The chat, Nabers said, wasn’t specifically about Thursday’s game but about the season in general. Part of it also involved working with Nabers to get him open to make plays.
“We were just talking about overall on the sideline, and just, they asked me what I see, asked me what calls and some of the calls would be just opportunities for us to get a unique play, whether it be me getting open or anybody else being open. So, just like I said, just letting the game come to us,” he said.
Nabers admitted that there are times when he gets in his own way and that he’s trying to work on not letting that consume what he brings to the table.
“I have my moments, but I continue to try to realize that I only can control the controllables,” he said. “I can’t just freely run any route I want. I have to run specifically the routes that I’m given.
“I got to be okay with having my opportunities and making those opportunities count. And just knowing when I got to help get somebody else open and help the team win as much as I can.”

title: Giants Week 10 Offensive Player Evaluations: Skattebo, Likely Deliver, Nabers Disappoints
full_text:
That’s how New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh summed up his team’s 24-21 loss to the Washington Commanders on Thursday night.
“It’s disappointing, yeah. I mean, I think that’s the best word. It’s just disappointing,” Harbaugh said after the game.
“We worked hard for this, and we put a hard week in. And we were prepared. The guys came out with, I thought, tremendous energy. We played very hard. Plays were made. Plays were missed. But it wasn’t good enough to win the game. And that’s the disappointment of it.”
Indeed, that sums it up nicely, particularly on offense, where the Giants outgained the Commanders 399 to 340 and averaged 6.2 yards per play to Washington’s 5.1.
But a 33.3% third-down conversion rate and points left on the field (kicker Dominic Zvada’s missed 33-yard chip shot comes to mind) reminded one of the dark ages when the Giants repeatedly proved they weren’t good enough to overcome their self-inflicted wounds.
Harbaugh, however, isn’t ready to throw in the towel.
“It’s disappointing, but you can’t let it bring you down,” he said. “We’re going to be good. We’re not going to curl up. We’re going to come out fighting.”
We can only hope. Meanwhile, here is a look at how each player on offense performed.
Talk about someone who deserved a better fate. We thought McCarthy played a winning game from start to finish, but his coordinator and head coach did not.
They let him down by turtling with the lead twice late in the game, taking the ball out of McCarthy’s hands.
We sure would have liked to see McCarthy get a chance to make a play on those two late-fourth-quarter possessions, but the coaches played conservatively and never let him.
Early on, he made most of his plays with his legs. A truly great improvisational play to get the ball to Cam Skattebo while being sacked led to a big, early 34-yard gain.
Later on, when his first two options were taken away on an RPO, he took off instead and got 12 yards, a really good decision.
On the negative side, Washington’s blitzes forced him to hurry his throws and nearly resulted in an interception. He then took a sack on a blitz after ignoring a wide-open Skattebo (who passed up the blitz pickup) in the flat.
A good scramble got him another 10 yards, and a sharp zone-read run added another 8. He finished the first half with a ho-hum 12-of-19 for 92 yards and just 7 points, but he still managed a solid four carries for 30 yards (7.5 average) on the ground.
In the second half, he started slinging it from the pocket. A 25-yard connection to Malachi Fields jump-started the offense on a third-quarter touchdown drive that gave his team a 14-10 lead.
His next possession started with another big play, a 37-yard layered deep out to Malik Nabers. Several snaps later, Nabers fumbled in the red zone, denying McCarthy another touchdown drive as the offense moved.
A dropped pass on a perfect throw to Theo Johnson ended another fourth-quarter drive.
Trailing 17-14, McCarthy then made his best throw of the night: a perfect dart against a blitzer right in his face into Isaiah Likely’s hands in the deep middle. Likely then took it into the end zone to complete a magnificent 66-yard touchdown play and put Washington up 21-17.
Two subsequent interceptions by the Giants’ defense should have closed out this game, but the coaches’ calls gave Washington one last chance to score. Washington took it. McCarthy finished with good numbers: 23 of 36 for 293 yards, one touchdown and just one sack.
One thing we wish McCarthy would push the coaches on: finding Skattebo in the flat, where he was open but ignored numerous times.
Bottom line: McCarthy played well enough Thursday night to win this game. His coaches did not.
The veteran backup converted his first of two tush pushes Thursday night. Still, the second, coming in the fourth quarter after the Jevon Holland interception, failed and forced a punt from deep in Giants territory on a three-and-out. That hurt.
We thought Skattebo played a really good multifaceted game. His 34-yard catch-and-run off a McCarthy improv play jump-started the sluggish offense early on.
Skattebo ran hard between the tackles, pushing piles consistently and getting the yards needed while showing no signs of the hamstring strain that kept him out of the previous week’s game.
His first touchdown of the night came from 1 yard out and was, in a word, tough. His second touchdown came on a cleanly executed pitch out wide, with a sharp cutback at the top of his run, knifing right through the hole for the score.
On the two late-game drives that turned into third-and-shorts, the coaches took the ball out of Skattebo’s hands, and failure resulted both times.
On several of those tough runs, we really wished he had a bit of jump in his lower body to bounce things outside in the hole. He set up the Washington middle with his toughness, but the lack of outside bounce kept things manageable for them, making the coaches’ short-yardage calls easy to stop.
Skattebo finished with 78 yards on 18 carries, a 4.3 average, and had 44 yards on three receptions. All night long, Skattebo was a beast in blitz pickup. We couldn’t find a single miss except on the sack, where there may have been a miscommunication.
One question, though: What was Skattebo doing, apparently taking the play off when Winston’s tush push failed late in the game? The quarterback needed a push, but no one was there.
Skattebo had a chance to get in behind Winston and push; that’s how these things work. Was it a simple brain freeze? That’s the only logical explanation we can come up with to explain him taking a play off at a critical moment.
Singletary got one early touch for 3 yards and then was run over in a pass-pro blitz pickup.
He barely got back on the field, as the offense with Skattebo looked so much more dangerous than Singletary.
The team’s No. 1 receiver's lack of playmaking reared its ugly head for the second game in a row. Last week it was a blatant drop of a perfect throw in the end zone plus a bunch of game-long hissy fits that don’t do anyone any favors.
This week it was another ho-hum line: five receptions for 44 yards (8.8 avg.), including one 37-yard deep sideline connection plus a handful of short, inconsequential catches.
Add in the game-killing third-quarter fumble on a 3-yard catch that was going nowhere, with his team trailing 17-14 and the offense on the move.
Add in a slip coming out of a break on a fourth-quarter route that sent the ball whistling to where he should have been. Add a fourth-quarter desperation heave against a zero blitz that was intercepted, as he not only failed to fight for the ball but did nothing to disrupt the interception.
Overall, it was a negative game from the Giants’ WR1 when they needed him to step up.
Continuing to produce solid results week in and week out, this rookie is as consistent as the day is long. He catches everything in his vicinity. This week he had three receptions for 62 yards (20.7 per catch) on just four targets.
He continues to block not only with physicality but with smarts. If a shield is all it will take to make a block, then he shields. If it’s a heavy block, then he sticks his nose into the contact and stands his ground.
He did miss one edge block Thursday night, but he was key on the 13-yard touchdown run and on several other plays. He probably deserves more targets since he is so strong and reliable. We’re still waiting on him to be a target on a jump ball or two. So far through nine games, zero jump balls.
Mooney made one big play, turning a third-down short crosser into a first down with a neat move that found a defensive back reaching for air.
On the night, he caught only two passes for 8 yards.
We couldn’t believe our eyes when we saw Likely suffer his first drop of the season on an early third down, as he tried to stop and double back against double coverage before running and securing the catch. We suppose, though, it had to happen sooner or later.
Undaunted, Likely went on…

title: Harbaugh Keeps the Faith After Another Costly Miss by Rookie Kicker
full_text:
There’s an adage that you don’t give up on talent the minute things head south, but with New York Giants rookie kicker Dominic Zvada, it’s fair to wonder when enough is enough.
In Thursday night’s 24-21 loss to the Washington Commanders, Zvada not only missed his lone field goal attempt, a 33-yarder from the troublesome right hash that was his sixth miss of the season and his first inside 40 yards, but also sent a kickoff out of bounds, gifting the Commanders starting field position on their own 40-yard line.
Those missed three points meant the difference between overtime and a loss.
Despite Zvada’s struggles, head coach John Harbaugh isn’t ready to pull the plug on his rookie kicker.
“You can’t, as soon as a guy doesn’t make a play, start firing people left and right. Especially your kicker who’s a rookie. So, I’m confident he’s going to become a good kicker,” Harbaugh said.
Harbaugh’s patience is admirable, but it’s also fair to wonder how many more mistakes he will tolerate.
The Giants, who for the most part this season have overcome their self-inflicted wounds, couldn’t do so in a key division game that, had they won, would have not only buried the Commanders but also padded the Giants’ fragile lead in the NFC East.
Zvada did make all three of his extra points, but after the game he told reporters that the 33-yard miss was one he should have made, blaming himself.
Still, he has his head coach’s confidence moving forward.
“I’m not going to panic halfway through the season when a guy’s made a bunch of kicks, if that’s what you’re inferring we should be doing,” Harbaugh said.
“We’re just not going to knee-jerk it like that. He’s going to make kicks. He’s going to make a lot of kicks. I believe in him. I think he’s really good and really talented. We’re going to allow him to do it, and it’s up to him to do it.”
The question is how much more opportunity the rookie will get before Harbaugh has no choice but to look elsewhere. It’s a question the head coach apparently hopes doesn’t come up again.

title: Giants Report Card: Lost Opportunity Against the Commanders
full_text:
Lost opportunity. That about sums up the New York Giants ’ 24-21 loss to the Washington Commanders on Thursday night.
The Giants had a chance to bury Washington’s 2026 season and further pad their hold on the NFC East ahead of a very difficult slate of opponents that begins next week with the Jacksonville Jaguars. Instead, the Giants threw it away, showing they’re still not ready for primetime exposure.
Let’s get into the unit grades for the week.
The Giants offense did a few things, but it wasn’t enough. Cam Skattebo was good, rushing for a team-leading 78 yards on 18 carries (4.3 average), but what was he thinking on that fourth-down tush push when he stayed in his stance for nearly two seconds before finally remembering to step up and help?
Tight end Isaiah Likely had another big game with nine catches for 127 yards and a touchdown, giving him a new career high of seven touchdowns in a season.
And J.J. McCarthy was even passable with a 23-of-36 showing for 293 yards and six carries for 34 yards.
But there was also a lot of bad that outweighed the good. Start with the 33.3% third-down conversion rate.
Throw in a miserable showing by receiver Malik Nabers, who had five receptions for 44 yards. He not only lost the first fumble of his career but also failed to try to break up the game-sealing interception by Commanders defensive back Rasul Douglas, then ducked out of the postgame locker room.
In the end, it wasn’t enough for the Giants offense despite gaining 399 yards and averaging 6.2 yards per play.
The safeties came to play this week, as both Jevon Holland and Ar’Darius Washington delivered key interceptions, and rookie Arvell Reese was once again a tackling machine, leading the defense with 13 tackles.
But for the second game in a row, Donte Banks failed to turn around to look for a ball deep downfield and was called for pass interference, which helped the Commanders win.
The pass rush was also missing in action, with two quarterback hits and a lone sack by defensive lineman Shelby Harris.
Dominic Zvada missed his first and only field goal attempt of the night, a 33-yarder that went wide left. The attempt came from the right hash, and we’re sorry, but if this young kicker can’t make field goals from either hash, regardless of conditions, then this team really needs to find someone who can.
Sticking with Zvada, he had a kickoff go out of bounds in the fourth quarter, gifting the Commanders excellent starting field position on their own 40-yard line. Thankfully, Holland’s interception snuffed out that scoring drive.
And the usually reliable Jordan Stout saved his worst punt of the night for last: a 12-yard lame duck that went out of bounds at the Commanders’ 29-yard line. Washington then mounted a four-play scoring drive for what was the game-winner.
Lastly, let’s talk about the return game. Punt returner Charlie Jones let a short punt bounce and roll backward, losing about 20 yards of field position in the process. Kickoff returner Gregory Derosiers showed no aggression on kickoffs and had a fumble to boot, though luckily the Giants recovered it.
Altogether, it was the worst showing of the season for the Giants’ special teams on a night when they needed this third phase of the game to step up.
We didn’t like the final series, in which the Giants, with two timeouts left, decided to pass instead of run. There was plenty of time to get the ball into field position, and the running game had been working well for the Giants, so why not stick with it?
The only reason we can think of is that they wanted to get into scoring position quickly and make things easier for their rookie kicker so they could play for the tie.
That said, those last two pass plays went to the right, which would have set up a field goal on the troublesome right hash if they’d gotten close enough. It made no sense.

title: D'Angelo Ponds Has Sudden Chance to Erase Jets' Concerns in Week 10
full_text:
Aaron Glenn and the New York Jets believe it's time to turn the starting nickel job over to their second-round rookie.
But if D'Angelo Ponds is going to take the next step in his development for his coach and team, merely getting starting reps will not be enough. New York's intended starter, Jarvis Brownlee, is dealing with an illness. If Ponds is to keep his job once Brownlee is back healthy, he'll need to produce.
The good news for New York is that a strong performance against the Buffalo Bills could give Ponds the confidence needed to begin to excel like many other players in the 2026 draft class.
Through the first two starts of his NFL career, Ponds has been a quality starter for New York. While Pro Football Focus has graded his outlook at a struggling 27.2, his coverage grades are far from that of a struggling player. He simply hasn't had enough snaps to see how good he can be.
In last week's loss to Kansas City, Ponds was targeted once, and gave up a reception for seven yards. He was also penalized for a second time this season that gave the Chiefs a first down. In his last start against the Miami Dolphins, though, Ponds was targeted three times, gave up one reception, and was called for a penalty that gave the opposition a first and goal.
The penalties are obviously a program, but these numbers are far from alarming example of Ponds being unable to perform. If anything, they highlight the fact he needs more reps to get comfortable on an NFL field.
"We can only play so many people. You see that across the league a number of hot picks... [Fernando] Mendoza hasn't played at all. We have some other good players on the team. He's going to get his shot. He's a damn good player. We all know that. Just be patient, and give him a little time. He's going to get a shot to play," Jets head coach Aaron Glenn said.
We have finally reached that part of the season with Ponds getting consistent playing time.
But context is also important. This is a rookie cornerback playing a new position (Ponds was used in the boundary during his college career), and didn't have a training camp to get acclimated. The bright spots shown on the field so far is what New York should be hoping to see.
He may not have broken out like Omar Cooper Jr. or David Bailey have, but Ponds seems on his way to being a productive member of the organization. He just needs the grace and time to be able to reach that mark.

title: 3 Logical Will McDonald IV Trade Destinations for the Jets This Offseason
full_text:
The Will McDonald IV experiment may be over after this season. The defensive end whom New York drafted 15th overall in 2023 requested a trade right before this year's deadline . While the Jets opted to keep McDonald, the writing may still be on the wall.
New York has three first-round picks in the 2027 NFL Draft. There has already been talk of Gang Green using one of those picks on a talent like Dylan Stewart or Colin Simmons. McDonald cited playing time as one reason for his request. It does not look like the road to more snaps is getting any shorter.
If the Jets decide to move on from McDonald this offseason, look for these names as potential suitors for the former first-round pick.
The Jaguars have already expressed interest for the Jets' edge rusher. Jacksonville allegedly made a "significant offer" for the defensive end before the trade deadline. It would be hard to believe they would lose interest before the offseason.
McDonald is a pure pass rusher. He wasn't drafted for his run-stopping abilities; rather, he was drafted for his ability to get to the passer. That ability would be well utilized on a Jacksonville team that has constantly been playing with a lead in 2026. Regardless of how the Jags finish their season, Will McDonald would be a good addition to a team hoping to contend for years to come.
Jacksonville should also be intrigued by landing a talent who has had a 10-sack season rather than drafting one next April. Jacksonville could address its middling offensive line in the draft if they send some capital to New York. McDonald was obviously appetizing to the team at the deadline, and that interest should hold as the year progresses.
McDonald could also find a new home in San Francisco this offseason. The former first-rounder was a pick from the Robert Saleh regime. A regime that developed roots in San Francisco. That connection could see McDonald in red and gold in 2027...
Saleh's defense still lingers in San Francisco. The former Jets head coach even returned to his old job with the 49ers before the Tennessee Titans hired him. McDonald could slot into a defense that is more like the one he was originally drafted to play. That, however, may not be the only reason the Jets and 49ers could find a trade.
The 49ers have had an injury bug that seems to have followed them for years. Nick Bosa has been one of the 49ers to be bitten. The former Defensive Player of the Year hasn't played a full season since 2023. Bosa is no doubt a lethal pass rusher, but that is only when he is actually on the field. McDonald would be welcome help for a team that always needs more bodies.
The Bears addressed a big need on the defensive line by trading a haul to Tennessee for Jeffery Simmons. Despite the deal's magnitude, Chicago still has holes on the outside of the line. There were some rumblings that the team would bring back Khalil Mack in a deal that ultimately did not go through.
Mack will be 36 next season; McDonald will be 28. If the Bears are looking to bolster their pass rush, a player like McDonald may be a perfect fit. McDonald is on a rookie deal that extends to next season, so Chicago could treat it as a prove-it deal if they so desire. The Bears are another team entering a championship window who could benefit from McDonald's talents.
An explosive edge like McDonald could be the perfect pairing with Ben Johnson's team. He is a young player who the team could either extend to ride out the championship window or drop him with little regret after 2027. Either way, McDonald could be an interesting watch if Chicago looks to shore up their d-line this offseason.

title: 3 Jets vs. Bills Matchups That Will Decide If New York Pulls Off the Week 10 Upset
full_text:
Coming off another disappointing loss, the Jets will look to get back on track when they host the Bills in Week 10. Buffalo has arguably been the best team in the league this season, led by 2024 MVP Josh Allen, who is making a strong case to win another with his performance this season.
Meanwhile, New York is on a four-game losing streak, and head coach Aaron Glenn’s hot seat continues to get warmer with each week . If Glenn wants to save his job, he’ll need to string together a few wins, particularly against the AFC East, where he’s compiled a 0-8 record.
For the Jets to pull off a miracle against the Bills, they must win these three key matchups.
Through nine weeks, Josh Allen is widely regarded as the front-runner for MVP thanks to his dual-threat dominance. The four-time Pro Bowler has been extremely efficient through the air, completing 66.1% of his passes for 2,057 yards, 12 touchdowns, and six interceptions.
He’s been equally dominant on the ground, leading all quarterbacks in rushing yards (285) and rushing touchdowns (9). Allen’s ability to make off-schedule throws, extend plays out of the pocket, and exploit opponents with his mobility makes him a defense’s worst nightmare.
Slowing Allen down will be a challenge for the Jets, considering their defense hasn’t done well this season. However, if New York wants to improve their chances of beating the Bills, it must keep Allen in the pocket and prevent him from hurting the defense with his legs.
We saw the Vikings do this on Monday night against Buffalo by bringing the house on Allen, blitzing him on 68.6% of his dropbacks and limiting him to just 15 yards on the ground. Although Minnesota lost, they held the Bills to their lowest-scoring total of the season (23) and sacked Allen four times.
Byron Murphy Jr. picks off Josh Allen 🔥 (via @NFL ) pic.twitter.com/8FrX0GWR8f
While the Jets don’t have pass rushers of similar caliber to the Vikings, they’ve had some success generating pressure this season. Through nine games, New York ranks 12th in sacks (22) and 13th in pressure rate (24%). They also boast one of the highest blitz rates, ranking third at 34%.
Simply sending an extra defender won’t be enough to contain Allen. The Jets can’t be undisciplined when blitzing, as Allen can hurt them with his mobility.
New York’s edge rushers must maintain the edge and not over-pursue Allen, something we’ve seen them struggle with against Malik Willis a couple of weeks back. The interior defenders and linebackers must also remain disciplined in their rush lanes and continue attacking the pocket, or the Jets won’t be able to collapse it.
Getting to Allen early will be critical, as we’ve seen him make costly mistakes when under pressure.
After getting to Allen a few times in the first quarter, the Vikings forced him to make an early decision that resulted in Byron Murphy making an incredible interception. If New York can force Allen into playing hero ball, it could create opportunities for turnovers and give the Jets a better chance of pulling off the upset.
The Jets insisted on keeping Breece Hall for several reasons; one was that he forms a dynamic backfield duo with Braelon Allen. Hall has explosive home-run play ability and is a great receiving back, while Allen is a physical downhill runner who excels at picking up yards after contact.
New York’s offense is at its best when it establishes the run, which opens up opportunities for offensive coordinator Frank Reich to dial up deep shots downfield. That was evident in the Jets’ wins over the Titans and Browns, as well as their narrow defeats to the Dolphins and Raiders. When the running game is clicking, the offense can dictate the tempo and keep opposing defenses on their heels.
However, we’ve only seen Hall and Allen play three full games this season. With Hall back, Reich must make a better effort to utilize both running backs and stick with the ground game, even if it doesn’t produce early. The Jets did this early against the Chiefs last week, particularly during their first few possessions, but abandoned the approach once they were down two scores.
Running the ball will be a challenge against the Bills. Buffalo ranks seventh in rushing yards allowed per game (91.6), 10th in yards per carry (3.9), and is tied for ninth in fewest rushes of 10-plus yards with 20. Over the last four games, they’ve allowed just 269 rushing yards.
Even though New York’s rushing attack hasn’t been as productive this season, ranking 20th in rushing yards per game (105.2), sticking with the run game will be critical in this matchup, along with finding ways to get their runners to the second level.
The Bills use a lot of five-down sets and rank 13th in stacked box rate, per Next Gen Stats. To counter this, New York should emphasize attacking the perimeter and bringing in extra blockers.
Reich has primarily used Jeremy Ruckert and Jelani Woods in multi-tight end sets when running the ball, and the pair have done well as run blockers. However, Reich must also consider doing this with Kenyon Sadiq and Mason Taylor to keep Buffalo guessing and prevent the offense from becoming predictable.
If the offensive line and extra blockers can clear a path for Hall and Allen to get to the outside on counters or sweeps, they could get to the second level and hurt Buffalo with their playmaking ability. Allen, in particular, would benefit from getting to the perimeter, where he has been effective at breaking tackles and picking up extra yardage.
Buffalo allows 3.4 yards after contact per attempt, the third-highest mark in the league. That could play right into Allen’s strengths and give him an opportunity to exploit one of the Bills’ biggest weaknesses.
While all eyes will be on David Bailey and Allen, among others, one of the most important individual matchups will be between Armand Membou and Gregory Rousseau.
Through the first eight weeks, Membou made a strong Pro Bowl case, giving up just two sacks and 16 pressures. However, that came to an abrupt halt last week , as he surrendered three sacks and four pressures against a Kansas City pass rush that was tied last in sacks (9) and ranked 29th in pressure rate (19.3%) entering the game.
The Jets desperately need Membou to bounce back this week against Rousseau, who’s been one of the most productive pass rushers this season. The former 2021 first-round selection leads the league in pressures (51), per Pro Football Focus , and is tied for second in sacks with eight.
Greg Rousseau's 8th sack of the season ties him for second in the league 😤 BUFvsMIN on ESPN⁰Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/OyIU25yJbs
New York’s top priority should be limiting Rousseau’s impact, as Buffalo’s other pass rushers have largely struggled to generate pressure. Behind Rousseau, Bradley Chubb and Deone Walker have combined for 50 pressures and just 2.5 sacks.
Even though Membou struggled last week, the Jets should not overreact to one bad outing and should have complete trust in their second-year tackle to hold his own against Rousseau. However, in obvious passing-down situations, New York should give him some extra help through double teams and have their tight ends chip Rousseau before releasing into their routes.
Reich also must consider mixing in some quick throws or screen passes to neutralize Rousseau and give time for Geno Smith to take downfield shots. Limiting Rousseau’s impact will be critical to giving Smith time to operate and preventing them from being in obvious passing situations.

title: Jets Shouldn't Hesitate to Throw VJ Payne Into the Fire If He Debuts vs. Bills
full_text:
After staying put at the trade deadline and deciding not to make any significant moves, the Jets turn their attention to a Week 10 home tilt against the Bills on Sunday as the second half of the NFL season gets underway.
Aside from the lack of adjustments and execution problems that continue to plague this coaching staff, injuries have been a recurring issue all season for Gang Green. That said, head coach Aaron Glenn provided an encouraging update on Friday that suggests this could be a much healthier team than it has been in a while.
"When it comes to injuries, the only person that'll be out will be Trevin Wallace ," Glenn said (h/t Jets). "Everybody else will be full: Jarvis Brownlee (Jr.), Harrison Phillips, Omar Cooper (Jr.), Joseph Ossai, Nahshon (Wright) and Garrett (Wilson). Garrett still has one more step to go through before he's cleared, and I see that happening. And then VJ Payne is still going through his process, so we'll see how that operates."
Coach Glenn provides an injury update ahead of #BUFvsNYJ pic.twitter.com/S3BPO6JHmo
That is a much better injury report than the Jets have had in recent weeks, and with back-to-back full practices under his belt, everything is pointing to rookie safety VJ Payne potentially making his NFL debut on Sunday after spending the start of the season on injured reserve due to a bone bruise in his knee.
His 21-day practice window has since been opened, and a potential return certainly appears to be on the horizon following the departure of former Jets safety Andre Cisco to the Lions.
Even though Payne was the last player selected in Gang Green's draft class after going 228th overall in the seventh round, the Jets should not hesitate to get him on the field as often as possible , even though he has not played yet.
After all, he has the speed, versatility and overall intangibles to be a solid contributor when that time comes and is more than deserving of getting an opportunity to show what he has, especially with the lack of depth that now exists on this roster.
To their credit, offseason acquisitions Dane Belton (76) and Minkah Fitzpatrick (53) rank second and fourth, respectively, in total tackles on the team this season and Fitzpatrick has the lone interception.
At the same time, the secondary has struggled with blown coverages and hasn't been the Jets' best unit. Combine that with the fact that Malachi Moore is the only depth piece they have behind them, and it becomes clear how much Payne's outlook could improve if he can have a strong showing when the opportunity comes his way.
The Jets have designated rookie safety VJ Payne to return from IR. Could help on kick coverage. pic.twitter.com/bnC5TMQeV4
While Glenn has doubled down on the process despite his 5-21 record in Gotham and an 0-8 divisional record against AFC East opponents, this season is lost at this point and it is not like they have much to worry about by putting an unproven rookie in Payne out there.
Not only will more snaps be available following the Cisco trade, but any snaps Payne potentially receives against an elite Bills offense could be a valuable learning experience.
While the Buffalo defense allows the fourth-most pass yards per game (238.8 ypg) and should give this offense some opportunities to exploit down the field , the Bills have the highest-scoring offense (32 ppg) and will present a stiff test for a struggling defense.
It is easy to point to the David Bailey vs. Arvell Reese debate after the Jets took the former with the No. 2 pick in the draft ahead of the latter (fifth overall to the Giants), but there is no reason to discredit and overlook Payne, either. By no means should he be compared to Bailey or have the immediate expectation of coming in and stealing the spotlight, but the lack of depth and lost season the Jets are experiencing should force their hand to put him out there and let him show what he has.
Regardless of Payne's status, it is hard to truly know what to expect from him as someone who has been sidelined all season. At this point, what do the Jets have to lose by throwing him into the fire and letting him get the full NFL experience against an explosive offense that can test him and find out what he is made of for the rest of this season and beyond?

title: 3-Round Jets Midseason 2027 Mock Draft: A Savior at QB & Dynamic Defenders
full_text:
The Jets are just two losses away from their 11th straight season of finishing below .500 . There are still eight games left this year.
Because of that, and due to the team looking at another loss on Sunday against the Bills, it's time to take at least a little bit of a peek at where the team could be drafting come April. Armed with three first-round picks and five picks in the top 70 overall selections, there's room to demand that the Jets be a busy franchise leading up to the 2027 draft.
So let's take an early look of what that will look like.
It may be too early to start throwing out mock drafts at this point. But with the Jets at 2-7 and with three first-round picks, the organization doesn't have to look far to find any sense of positivity for its future.
For a fanbase devoid of much to look forward to, a mock draft like this could provide some solace that their struggles may be at an end... in 2027.
New York does not need to trade up to get their quarterback. If the draft stays the way it is, Notre Dame captain and signal-caller CJ Carr will fall right into their laps , and the Jets would come away with the best pure pocket passer of the class.
Carr is a player with excellent accuracy and a good enough arm to make every throw in the NFL. While he isn't the most mobile player, his comparisons to Brock Purdy are fair: someone who makes plays when he needs to and is deadly accurate when in rhythm.
Trust and execution. That’s CJ being CJ ☘️ #GoIrish ☘️ | @13Cjcarr pic.twitter.com/0UrB1aW1U1
While some Jets fans will be disappointed that the team will miss out on Drew Mestemaker, the organization should be thrilled with a pick like this.
The math is there. The Jets should be able to get their quarterback of the future and a top edge rusher in their current situation. In this mock, Simmons is the one who falls, and Stewart goes earlier.
Simmons is a complete edge player—someone who has the speed, power, and willingness to stop the run. He would fit well in New York's defense along with David Bailey and could be another transcendent player along the defensive line.
If the Jets can pair their star rookie with another edge rusher, it would change how teams attack them going forward.
The two big positions of need on draft day for the Jets will be at quarterback and defensive line. They must add two new pieces along the line, and a quarterback as well. With the 13th pick, the Jets end up taking an excellent playmaker along their interior in Echoles.
This is another player who could very well be unavailable when the team makes this pick, but if New York can get an edge rusher and a top tackle, this will be an A+ draft, especially with someone as complete as Echoles is at both pass rush and run defense.
I wouldn't be surprised if Jones goes a lot earlier than this. However, the size (6'4") and speed are something that the Jets could simply fall in love with, regardless of who the coach is going forward. Jones has been a key part of Mississippi State this season and has the ability to be the kind of lockdown corner the Jets are missing.
New York gets a center to potentially replace Josh Myers in the third round.
Boswell hasn't allowed a sack in two seasons at Houston, but he does have a penalty problem that will need to be addressed. He fits well with the modern look of a center and is plenty athletic. He could compete for a starting job right away.

title: Jets Tease Much-Needed Offensive Shift Ahead of Week 10 Bills Showdown
full_text:
There's an unfortunate stigma surrounding Aaron Glenn as the Jets' head coach . One that follows many defensive-minded coaches.
His Jets are too conservative.
Glenn's in-game decision is highlighted most by his willingness not to be as aggressive as his bravado may suggest. Whether it's kicking field goals at the goal line instead of going for touchdowns, or failing to attack downfield as part of an offensive game plan, the Jets have consistently found themselves in close games with a coach trying hard not to lose.
Perhaps that is just another reason why the Jets are 2-7 on the year .
But heading into another AFC East clash— this one against the Bills on Sunday —the Jets may be shifting their philosophy. They need to if they want any shot at beating their arch-rivals.
For a coach who worked under Lions leader Dan Campbell, it's a bit surprising that Glenn has been as conservative as he's been as a head coach. He ranks near the bottom of the league when it comes to opting against analytics in "coin flip" situations.
But that could be changing on Sunday. It will have to when they take on Josh Allen and the Bills.
Speaking to reporters on Thursday, offensive coordinator Frank Reich explained that the team knows they'll need to be more aggressive, especially on fourth down, if they hope to keep pace with Buffalo's high-powered offense.
Buffalo's offense is first in the league in points scored and first in the league in total yards. Head coach Joe Brady's infusion has turned Buffalo into an even bigger Super Bowl threat than before.
But with Buffalo's strength also comes a weakness. Their defense, especially their secondary, ranks 29th against the pass. Part of that could be based on the team having such large leads that they force opponents to throw the ball, but the numbers are clear:
New York must stretch the ball downfield in order to keep pace with its rival's offense.
That's the other philosophical change the team must make. It's not just about going for it on fourth down every time they are close, but it's also about pushing the ball downfield and challenging Buffalo's corners on the outside.
The Jets have the weapons to do so. Garrett Wilson, the Jets' leading receiver, is expected to return from a concussion last week. Omar Cooper Jr. and Adonai Mitchell are also quality weapons for the team to use.
Omar Cooper Jr. is the first rookie this season to win Rookie of the Week twice 🔥 @Pepsi pic.twitter.com/vDwuVTrd1k
There can be no excuse for the Jets offense not to show up on Sunday. And if the team is going to keep pace, they'll need one of their best games from a coaching and production standpoint.
It's time to get aggressive.
